blocks.text: BAGUIO CITY — A portion of Kennon Road at Camp 5 was temporarily closed on Sunday, Aug. 30, due to falling rocks amid continuous rains, according to a road advisory.

The advisory warned motorists, commuters and pedestrians of continuing erosion and urged them to exercise extra caution when passing through affected areas of the century-old road, which spans almost 34 kilometers from the boundary of La Union province to Baguio.
By 5 p.m., the road was closed at Camp 5.
As of 7 a.m. on Aug. 31, one lane at Camp 5 had become passable, but Kennon Road remained open only to residents.
A 10 a.m. update said clearing operations were ongoing at Camp 5, with assistance from barangay officials and barangay tanods.
Authorities continued to remind the public to remain alert for possible road hazards, avoid unnecessary travel during heavy rainfall, and follow safety advisories. /mcm

articles.title: Bojie Dy calls on Filipinos to contribute to building a better country
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — As the country observed National Heroes’ Day on Monday, Speaker Faustino “Bojie” Dy III called on Filipinos to contribute to nation-building in ways big or small, while…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — As the country observed National Heroes’ Day on Monday, Speaker Faustino “Bojie” Dy III called on Filipinos to contribute to nation-building in ways big or small, while remaining compassionate and unwavering.
Dy made this call as he reminded Filipinos that National Heroes’ Day is not simply a day of commemoration, but a period to remind Filipinos of who they are.
This, he said, is the vital legacy of the country’s heroes—the belief that there are things far more important than the self, the nation and the future of the next generation.
“Ngayon, tayo naman ang may pananagutan na ipagpatuloy ang pamana na iyon (now, it is our responsibility to carry on that legacy),” said Dy in a statement.

“Sa isang panahon na mabilis magbago ang mundo, kailangan nating bumalik sa mga pagpapahalagang hindi dapat magbago: katapatan sa salita at gawa, paggalang sa kapwa, malasakit sa nangangailangan, tapang na panindigan ang tama, at pagmamahal sa bayan,” he added.

(In a time when the world changes rapidly, we must return to values that should remain constant: integrity in word and deed, respect for others, compassion for the needy, the courage to stand up for what is right, and love for country.)
He reminded the public that one does not need to be famous or perform extraordinary deeds to be a hero. They simply need to choose to be honorable “every day at every opportunity.”
“Dahil ang isang mas maunlad at matatag na Pilipinas ay hindi lamang itinatayo ng mga lider. Itinatayo ito ng bawat Pilipinong may malasakit at paninindigan,” said Dyy.
(For a more prosperous and resilient Philippines is not built by leaders alone; it is built by every Filipino who possesses compassion and conviction.)
“Alalahanin natin ang mga bayani ng ating nakaraan at higit sa lahat mahalin natin ang ating bayan at kapwa upang lalo pang pagtibayin ang Pilipinas na kanilang ipinaglaban,” he added.
(Let us honor the heroes of our past, and above all, let us love our country and our fellow citizens, further strengthening the Philippines they fought for.) /mr

articles.title: Goodbye to Babylon Berlin, the 1920s TV drama that has eerily foreshadowed real-life politics
articles.summary:
The long-running drama reaches Hitler’s rise to power in its final season as its creators reflect on the unsettling parallels between Weimar Germany and the present day

It’s the global hit…

blocks.text: It’s the global hit TV series that pulled audiences straight into the chaotic hedonism of 1920s Germany, dramatising the brilliance and brittleness of a newly built democratic system with unprecedented ambition.

But in the 13 years that the German makers of Babylon Berlin have worked on the show, modern democracies from the US to Hungary to South Korea have come under pressure in ways the creators say they could never have imagined when they started.

Now they are preparing to unveil the fifth and final season, culminating in Adolf Hitler’s rise to power, the same week that Germany will face one of the biggest tests of its postwar order in a watershed state election.
The timing, they insist, is pure coincidence, but is fitting for an ambitious programme set a century ago during the Weimar republic that has always felt eerily prescient.
As the team gets ready to sign off, the inexorable end of the story is now upon the familiar characters of the noirish police procedural, with its lush period sets and frisson of impending doom.

“It’s no longer a dance on the rim of the volcano,” said lead actor Liv Lisa Fries, using a German idiom for the explosion of avant garde culture and sexual liberation in the 1920s before the descent into fascism. “We’re in the volcano itself.”

Fries plays the series’ intrepid working-class heroine Charlotte Ritter, who works her way up from secretarial duties and underworld sex work to become the first female detective on the Berlin police force.

Her co-star Volker Bruch is Gereon Rath, a shellshocked first world war veteran whose eventful odyssey through the trauma of his era bears a resemblance to Christopher Nolan’s summer blockbuster, The Odyssey.
But the more striking parallel is Germany in 2026.

blocks.caption: Power struggle … episode 12 of series four of Babylon Berlin. Photograph: Frédéric Batier/ARD/Sky Studios

blocks.text: The far-right Alternative für Deutschland, an extremist, anti-constitutional party founded around the same time that work on the series began, is now leading national opinion polls.

On Sunday 6 September, it could win its first absolute majority in a state election, in Saxony-Anhalt, and two weeks later may beat its opponents in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern. In Berlin, it is polling close to the far-left party Die Linke.

With German democracy facing such a stress test, Bruch said the political “parallels” jumped out. But he resisted overly simplistic comparisons, citing an old adage: “History doesn’t repeat itself that way – it rhymes.”
The blurred lines between life and art took on sometimes surreal dimensions during the course of the production.

Series three was filmed in part at the neo-baroque Villa Adlon, which in November 2023 served as the real-life venue for a secret meeting of AfD officials and neo-Nazis to discuss a “remigration” plan for mass deportations if the party came to power.
Series five sees Hitler’s appointment as Reich chancellor, just as an medical file goes missing that casts new light on his time as a soldier in the first world war.
Although it was always clear how the series would end, watching Babylon Berlin has meant hoping to the last that history would take another turn.
That poignancy transformed a sophisticated crime show into something more affecting, and perhaps more enduring.
Across 50-odd hours, the show, based partly on a series of novels by Volker Kutscher, helped expand the scale and ambition of European television drama.
“It was almost impossible even then when they started,” said Scott Roxborough, the European bureau chief of entertainment trade magazine the Hollywood Reporter.

It was the product of a “pioneer time”, he said, when Germany was willing to throw massive resources at a chance to catch up with splashy shows from the US and Britain like Breaking Bad and The Crown.

“I think it would be almost impossible to do it nowadays unless an Apple TV or a Netflix decided to finance everything,” something he said was increasingly unlikely as the global streaming companies take a more cautious, profits-first approach.
Babylon Berlin has reached audiences around the world – 140 countries at last count – with its cautionary tale of a vibrant civilisation’s inherent fragility.
“The secret to the series’s success in capturing the zeitgeist is definitely not that it mirrors the present. I don’t believe that,” one of its three creators, Tom Tykwer, said.

Rather, audiences have been drawn to the “transformative force” of Berlin in the 1920s, when a weak government and a churning society left room for women, gay people and new immigrants to rewrite the rules.
“That brings forth an incredible number of wonderful, positive, beautiful blossoms, but because it’s so experimental, they’re also destroyed again almost immediately,” he said.
“We’ve tried to explore the universal themes that stem from the fact that political systems are people-centred so are always under threat. It will always be that way.”

Tykwer also co-composed much of the original music for the series, including the haunting theme song To Ashes, to Dust. The fifth season features a plot excursion to Paris and an on-screen rendition of the tune by French neo-chanson star Zaho de Sagazan.

In series five, Tykwer and his team have also revived the 1920 queer anthem Das Lila Lied with its rousing chorus “Wir sind nun einmal anders als die andern” (We’re just different from the others) for the series.

It is rousingly sung in a nightclub frequented by cross-dressing patrons and uniformed, gay SA officers – a startling melange the producers say was not uncommon before the brutal Nazi crackdown on the LGBTQ+ community.

While Tykwer bristles at the notion that the series should deliver any sort of “message” to Germans about their choices at the ballot box this month, fellow creator Henk Handloegten said he was proud to have “struck a nerve” with audiences around the world who find themselves at a political crossroads.
“I believe that we’ve taken a clear political stand, even now in the final series, and I find it very necessary,” he said.
For Handloegten, the pressure on democracy in many countries where the show is watched, “has really motivated me”.

“It’s given me the justification to engage with [this era] for so long and so deeply, because I felt there was a relevance to it in today’s world. And for me, in a strange way, that’s political work – something we’ve been doing here for 13 years now.”

articles.title: Trump still teases a third presidential run, but he's talking more and more about life after 2028
articles.summary: WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump has frequently suggested he wants to seek a third term, posting about mounting another campaign, donning 2028 caps and discussing ways to make it happen —…

blocks.text: U.S. President Donald Trump waves from his official vehicle as he heads to attend the 47th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit after arriving at Kuala Lumpur International Airport in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, Sunday, Oct. 26, 2025. (Hasnoor Hussain/Pool Photo via AP/File)

WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump has frequently suggested he wants to seek a third term, posting about mounting another campaign, donning 2028 caps and discussing ways to make it happen — even as he's acknowledged the Constitution prohibits it.
But lately, Trump has begun showing signs that even he doesn't really believe another run will happen.

During recent speeches, the Republican president has begun describing life after the White House when his term ends in January 2029, predicting he'll be at home and agonizing as his successor claims credit for his accomplishments.

“Your next president is going to say, ‘What a great job I did,’” Trump told an event on Long Island, New York, this month. “He’ll be sitting around, watching television. A real stiff. Unless you vote Republican, of course.”

A sitting president talking about becoming a former one is always politically fraught. But with midterm elections now just nine weeks away, Trump is approaching the point of his presidency where there will be more and more reminders that his power will soon wane.

Being willing to say he's contemplating a White House without him marks a notable shift for Trump. Going back to his first term and from virtually the moment he won a second, he's left the door open to staying put for more than eight years.

“He is all over the place,” said Brian Kalt, a Michigan State University constitutional law professor. “And what that does is, it allows him to point to his own words to support any number of mutually exclusive things.”
Trump can say, “’Oh yeah, I made it clear that I wasn’t gonna run,'” Kalt said. “Or, if he decides that he will, he could say, ’Well, you know, I never said I wouldn’t.’”
Trump suggests his post-presidency may make him cry

The White House dismissed suggestions that Trump's thoughts are increasingly turning to the clock running out on his presidency — and the legacy he'll leave behind. Spokesperson Olivia Wales said he “is fighting every day” to deliver on promises to reduce violent crime, crackdown on the U. S-Mexico border, and lower prescription drug prices.
“The only legacy President Trump is concerned with is making America greater than ever before,” Wales said.
Still, hinting at how he'll be remembered is something Trump is suddenly talking about a lot.

During a recent Pennsylvania rally, he said, “Whoever the next president is, he's going to be talking about what a brilliant president he is. And I’ll be home. And I’ll be saying, ’That son of a gun,' because we did the job.”
A week later in Georgia, Trump was predicting that once his presidency was over, “I’ll be sitting home.”
“I may be crying,” the president added, arguing that Democrats could retake the Senate and scrap filibuster rules, making it easier to move their key legislation.
Then, in Michigan, Trump injected some doubt into whether he was ready to hand over the Oval Office and move back to Florida.
“In two and a half years, you may have a different president — may,” he said, emphasizing the “may.”

“I’ll be sitting home. I’ll be reading the papers. I’ll be watching television,” Trump said, before swiping at his predecessor, President Joe Biden. “And I’ll be having some guy — like last time, a real idiot — stand up and say, ‘We are doing record business.'”
Mixed Trump signals are still most common
But even as he's begun to suggest he'll be leaving the presidency, Trump has also continued to tease a 2028 reelection run.

Addressing the rescheduled White House Correspondents' Association dinner last month, Trump joked, “Just like my presidency, the second time is always better” and that “the third time will be better yet. I’m only kidding.” He later wore a 2028 campaign cap to finish the speech.

The Constitution’s 22nd Amendment says no one can be elected president more than twice. It was ratified in 1951, six years after President Franklin Delano Roosevelt died, months into his fourth term. Until Roosevelt, no other president had defied the tradition of stepping down after two terms that George Washington started.
Still, Trump had only been back in the White House for a couple of months when he told NBC News, “There are methods which you could” use to seek a third term.
He acknowledged that one method was to be the running mate to Vice President JD Vance in 2028 — then have Vance step aside if the pair won.
“There are others, too,” Trump said then, alluding to more options. He later told Time Magazine, “There are some loopholes,” while also saying he didn't believe in using them.
The president has since often used his social media posts to promote “Trump 2028” logos featuring his slogan “Make America Great Again.”
But Trump has also at times seemed definitive about the ban on him making another run, acknowledging recently to reporters: “I’d love to run, but the law is very strong.”
Kalt wrote about a two-term president possibly getting back to office by running for vice president in “constitutional Cliffhangers: A Legal Guide for Presidents and Their Enemies.”
“People do tend to find, in Trump’s words, whatever it is that they want to hear,” he said.
Trump may be fighting the ‘lame duck’ factor

Second-term presidents typically see their power and influence wane during their last two years, particularly if their party suffers big midterm defeats. But Trump's comments could also be a sign he's thinking about cementing his legacy, a stage that many of his predecessors also reached.
“They all, particularly as they cross the midpoint of their second term, start thinking about legacy,” said Paul Begala, a former adviser to President Bill Clinton.

“They all banish the word. I know Clinton and Bush, they said, ’Can’t use the L-word.' But they do,” Begala said, referring to his old boss Clinton and to President George W. Bush. “They all think about it. And the staff thinks about it and the Cabinet thinks about it.”

In his last two years of office, Clinton threw himself into trying to broker a Middle East peace agreement. Bush used the slogan “sprint to the finish” during his presidency's final year in 2008, and Biden adopted a “run through the tape” ethos after abandoning his reelection bid.
Trump has leaned into molding the White House and Greater Washington in his own image, harkening back to his days as a real estate developer in 1970s and 1980s New York.

He's ordered up a towering arch near the Lincoln Memorial and restored city fountains, while constructing a Rose Garden patio area and helipad on the White House lawn and adding scores of gilded touches to the building’s stately interior and exterior.

And then, there's the massive ballroom that Trump has crews rushing to finish in the face of legal challenges — a project the president says will only be completed late in 2028, shortly before he leaves office.

“It’s not for me, 'cause I’m going to be here a very short period of time” when the work is finished, Trump recently told reporters in the Oval Office. “I’ll be there for four, five, six months. This is for future presidents.”

articles.title: BCDA grants original proponent status for ₱5-billion New Clark City water system
articles.summary: The joint venture of Maynilad Water Services Inc. and South Korean firm Korea Water Resources Corp. (K-Water) has secured original proponent status (OPS) for its ₱4.8-billion proposal to manage water…

blocks.text: The joint venture of Maynilad Water Services Inc. and South Korean firm Korea Water Resources Corp. (K-Water) has secured original proponent status (OPS) for its ₱4.8-billion proposal to manage water and wastewater services in New Clark City, Tarlac.
In a statement, the Bases Conversion and Development Authority (BCDA) said it granted the status on Aug. 28 following an unsolicited proposal from the joint venture.

The project will now undergo the standard public-private partnership (PPP) approval process before proceeding to a Swiss challenge, where the OPS holder retains the right to match competing offers submitted by other qualified private sector proponents.
Subject to necessary approvals and the PPP process, the BCDA plans to award the contract in December. The public utility component will be operated by a duly qualified entity.
Maynilad and K-Water are proposing a long-term water supply and wastewater management framework to strengthen utility capacity and establish sustainable infrastructure in New Clark City.

“We are building New Clark City for the decades ahead. That means putting in place the basic systems that will allow businesses to invest, communities to grow, and the city to manage its resources responsibly,” said BCDA President and Chief Executive Officer (CEO) Joshua Bingcang.

Bingcang noted earlier this year that the project would boost New Clark City's water capacity to between 150 million and 200 million liters per day, up from its current 20 million to 30 million liters per day. Maynilad currently operates the city's water supply under a short-term contract set to expire this year.

The BCDA expects the added capacity to meet rising demand from residential, commercial, institutional, and industrial developments. An integrated water and wastewater system will also support high-value economic activities, including advanced manufacturing and data centers.

“Growth requires infrastructure that can keep up with it. Water and wastewater are fundamental to that growth, and we want New Clark City to have a system that is reliable, sustainable, and built to meet the needs of the metropolis for the long term,” Bingcang added.

Securing reliable water and wastewater infrastructure is crucial as the BCDA seeks to attract investments in advanced manufacturing, particularly through its proposed Pax Silica artificial intelligence industrial hub. Situated within New Clark City, the hub aims to draw investments in AI-supporting technologies—such as electronics and semiconductors—that demand a massive water supply.

articles.title: Leaders of China, Russia and India are among heads of state meeting to counter US influence
articles.summary: The leaders of China, Russia and India are among the heads of state gathering in Kyrgyzstan this week for the summit of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization, a group billed as a counterweight to…

blocks.text: Russian President Vladimir Putin, left, gestures while speaking to Chinese President Xi Jinping during the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit in Samarkand, Uzbekistan, Sept. 16, 2022. (Sergei Bobylev, Sputnik, Kremlin Pool Photo via AP, File)

The leaders of China, Russia and India are among the heads of state gathering in Kyrgyzstan this week for the summit of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization, a group billed as a counterweight to U.S. global influence.
Chinese President Xi Jinping, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi are scheduled to attend the events in Bishkek, the capital of the Central Asian nation.

Multiple one-on-one meetings are scheduled on its sidelines, including one between Putin and Xi on Monday, as well as talks between the Russian leader and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on Tuesday, the day of the official SCO sessions.

Russia, now 4½ years into its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, and Iran, six months into a war with the United States and Israel, see the summit as an important platform to strengthen their relations with non-Western partners.

The SCO was founded in 2001 by China, Russia and four Central Asian states as a security forum. Over the past quarter-century, it has grown in size and influence, although its goals and programs remain vague and its brand recognition low.
It now includes 10 nations: Russia, China, India, Iran, Pakistan, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan. Many other countries have the status of “dialogue partners."

Along with Russia, China has presented the SCO as an alternative to Western-aligned organizations like the G7, and in recent years has wanted to expand the scope and influence of the organization, pledging development and financial assistance.

China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said last week that the organization has successfully “explored a new path for regional cooperation.” Beijing has consistently promoted the idea of an alternative world order with Russia’s support.
Summit attendees have significant disagreements
For many SCO members, the summit will be an opportunity to show that they maintain strong ties on the global stage despite souring relations with the West.
The organization is not a unified political or military bloc, however, and analysts note that its members have significant disagreements and their own distinct interests.
For countries such as India, however, experts say the summit is likely to be more about optics and strategic signaling than substantive outcomes.
The forum is heavily influenced by China and includes Pakistan as a member — both of which are rivals for India.

Dinakar Peri, a fellow in security studies at Carnegie India, said the SCO gives India a seat at the table in a region increasingly shaped by competition among the larger powers, allowing it to protect its interests, track shifting geopolitical currents and project itself as a reliable stakeholder.
“While it may not entirely shape the agenda, it gives New Delhi a first-hand view of the region and allows it to hedge its position with others,” Peri said.
Turkey, which holds partner status within the SCO, also seeks to use the platform to strengthen its position in the region.
It views SCO membership as part of a balanced foreign policy that seeks to maintain its traditional ties with the West as a part of NATO, while strengthening its influence in Eurasia.

President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, who brought his country into the SCO as a “dialogue partner” in 2012, has repeatedly stated that he wants Turkey to become a permanent member. While Turkey has close trade ties with the European Union under a 1995 trade deal, its EU membership bid has stalled for more than 25 years.

articles.title: VP Sara trial continues Tuesday with 2 AFP officers as witnesses
articles.summary: Two Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) officers are expected to take the witness stand Tuesday, Sept. 1 during day 20 of Vice President Sara Duterte's Senate impeachment trial, as the prosecutors…

blocks.text: Two Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) officers are expected to take the witness stand Tuesday, Sept. 1 during day 20 of Vice President Sara Duterte's Senate impeachment trial, as the prosecutors try to expose details of the alleged misuse of P112.5 million in Department of Education (DepEd) confidential funds.

Colonels Manaros Boransing II and Magtangol Panopio are scheduled to testify before the Senate impeachment court on military certifications that DepEd used in responding to Commission on Audit (COA) findings on its confidential fund expenditures.
The certifications are significant to the prosecution because they were linked to activities cited by DepEd in accounting for its confidential funds, including Youth Leadership Summits (YLS).
Respondent Duterte was the concurrent DepEd secretary from 2022 to 2024.

During a House panel investigation in 2024, military officers whose certifications were obtained by DepEd testified that their units did not receive DepEd confidential funds for the activities covered by the documents.

House impeachment team adviser and spokesperson Robert Ace Barbers said the prosecution intends to establish the circumstances surrounding the certifications and how they came to be used in answering audit questions on public funds.
The issue involves P15 million in DepEd confidential funds that was linked in House proceedings to YLS conducted by military units.

Boransing was originally scheduled to testify last Wednesday, Aug. 26, but sought the postponement of his appearance because he needed to coordinate with his military superiors before leaving his post.

The court's presiding officer, Senator Francis “Chiz” Escudero granted the request, citing the “exigencies of his position” as commanding officer of the AFP's Task Force Zamboanga, and reset his appearance to Sept. 1.
Panopio is also scheduled to testify Tuesday.

The two officers are among the witnesses called by the prosecution after former DepEd special disbursing officer (SDO) Edward Fajarda, who had been lined up as a hostile witness, became temporarily unavailable because of his reported medical condition.
Fajarda remains on the prosecution’s witness list, with Sept. 7 earlier reserved for his possible testimony, subject to his condition and an assessment by the Senate Medical and Dental Bureau.

The prosecution had also sought the testimony of retired Maj. Gen. Adonis Bajao but later dispensed with him as a witness after difficulties in serving a subpoena because his address could not be established.
The Vice President has never attended the proceedings.
Michael Poa
Tuesday’s hearing could also put one of Duterte’s own lawyers on the witness stand.

Michael Poa, Duterte’s former DepEd chief of staff and spokesperson who is now a member of her impeachment defense team, is formally scheduled to testify for the prosecution on Wednesday. Escudero, however, said Poa could be called as early as Tuesday if either Boransing or Panopio fails to appear.

“Given that Atty. Poa is here and more than willing to testify, as intimated earlier, then we jump to Atty. Poa, should the other earlier two witnesses fail to appear on Sept. 1, without need of issuing a subpoena to Atty. Poa,” Escudero said during last week’s hearing.
The prosecution has said it will ask the impeachment court to declare Poa a hostile witness because he is now part of Duterte’s defense team.
Poa served as Duterte’s chief of staff and spokesperson when she was education secretary and was involved in DepEd’s response to COA findings concerning its confidential funds.

He also had a role in obtaining and submitting the military certifications and was previously identified in House proceedings as having material information on the preparation of accomplishment reports involving DepEd confidential fund expenditures.
If the impeachment court grants the prosecution’s request, Poa would become the third witness declared hostile in the confidential fund misuse charge against Duterte.

articles.title: Rescue efforts intensify after Nepal-Tibet flooding as deaths climb past 900
articles.summary: KATHMANDU, Nepal (AP) — Authorities were intensifying rescue efforts after catastrophic flooding in Nepal and Tibet killed at least 900 people and left more than 4,700 missing. “We are working in…

blocks.text: A drone view shows a major section of Pasang Lhamu highway washed away along swollen Trishuli river by recent flash floods cutting off Rasuwa district from Nuwakot area, Nepal, Monday, Aug. 31, 2026. (AP Photo/Rajesh Kumar Singh)
KATHMANDU, Nepal (AP) — Authorities were intensifying rescue efforts after catastrophic flooding in Nepal and Tibet killed at least 900 people and left more than 4,700 missing.
“We are working in search and rescue of the stranded people from hills, settlements and river areas,” said Brig. Gen. Raja Ram Basnet, Nepal’s army spokesman.
Multiple foreign teams were also assisting local rescuers to find trapped workers in hydropower tunnels. Officials say at least 90 people are trapped in multiple tunnels of hydropower plants.

Nepal’s disaster agency said Monday that 903 deaths had been counted in that country, with 4,247 people, including 592 foreigners, missing. As of Sunday, Chinese authorities reported 16 deaths and 546 missing, and Chinese state media said 261 of the missing were foreigners, including over a hundred Nepalis.

Wednesday’s flash floods started after a glacial collapse high in the Himalayan region. Scientists who studied satellite images said bedrock underneath a glacier high in the Himalayan region had collapsed, taking part of the glacier with it. The rockfall was so extreme that it registered as a magnitude 5.2 seismic event.
The rocks and melted water then swelled the rivers in the valleys below, causing a torrent of water that swept buildings, bridges and earth downstream in Tibet and Nepal.
Authorities in Nepal warned of possible fresh flooding and urged residents in flood-affected districts to remain on high alert after water levels rose in the Bhotekoshi River.

The latest warnings came after Chinese authorities informed their Nepalese counterparts of increased water flow upstream, according to Dharam Raj Uprety, chief executive of Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority.
The Chinese state news agency Xinhua, citing the country’s water resources ministry, said a new lake formed after Wednesday’s floods high in the mountains had largely drained.

But Xinhua said the ministry warned that a crater located 5.6 kilometers (3.5 miles) upstream, which held an estimated 1.4 million cubic meters (370 million gallons) of water, still posed some risk and required close monitoring.

The missing include hundreds of people from over a dozen countries who were in the region to work, visit the mountains or make a pilgrimage to a sacred peak. On Sunday, Chinese state media said 261 foreigners were missing in Tibet, including over a hundred Nepalis and others from around the world.
Some are returning to what remained of their homes
In Dhading, one of the worst-hit regions in Nepal, some residents began returning to ruined homes to see what can be salvaged.

Residents sat in homes with walls washed away by the floods, shoveling sludge-like mud and rubble off balconies or window frames. Others scanned the ground for items they could pick out of the mud and rinse off. One man had returned for his chickens, which he found alive. He tied them up and put them in the cabin of his truck.
“Everything is finished. Nothing is left. Not even our home,” Sharmila Tamang, a Dhading resident who was trying to salvage items from her home, told The Associated Press.
At a key power plant that was severely damaged by the floods, workers started inspecting the facilities Sunday to survey the destruction. The plant serves over 20,000 people across four districts.

In the town of Galchhi, a group of residents sought higher ground on a nearby bridge and watched as the river roared by. Some pointed to enormous rocks washed downriver during the earlier floods, while others standing on a suspension bridge were warned off with whistles.

Along the river, homes, vehicles and farm tractors could be seen jutting from the thick gray-brown sediment that enveloped entire villages in some areas. Parts of rice terraces along the riverside had dropped into the river after landslides hit them.
Residents are receiving constant flood warnings
Homes and businesses left intact after the flooding were still without electricity on Sunday, as twisted power line poles and wires lay tangled in the mud.
Residents of flood-hit villages said they were struggling to make sense of near-constant alarms they've received since the initial floods.

“Sometimes they say a flood is coming, then we have to run again to higher ground, even at night. There is also rain,” said Govind Shreshta, a resident. “It’s really difficult for me. I have a 72-year-old father and 70-year-old mom. I must carry them and I am exhausted. It’s going on like this for those who are still alive.”
Large concrete and smaller suspension bridges were destroyed, leaving communities on the other side of the river with less easy access.

“Those who are there are now stuck there. Those who are here are stuck here. It’s going to be very difficult,” said Sattan Singh Tamang, 47, who was working near a bridge when Wednesday’s floods came.

articles.title: Alex Eala fever hits US Open
articles.summary: From her practice sessions to exhibition and mixed doubles matches, there is no doubt that Alex Eala is a crowd favorite in the ongoing U. Open, drawing thousands of fans who flock to the courts just…

blocks.text: From her practice sessions to exhibition and mixed doubles matches, there is no doubt that Alex Eala is a crowd favorite in the ongoing U. Open, drawing thousands of fans who flock to the courts just to catch a glimpse of the Filipina star.

The 21-year-old Eala humbly acknowledged the reality of her meteoric rise, embracing it with a grateful heart while recognizing that her breakthrough was perhaps inevitable, given the historic distinction of becoming the first Filipina to achieve such an impressive feat.
“At the forefront of everything is gratitude: I’m very grateful for the support that my fans give me and that my supporters give me,” Eala said.
“Every single WTA player and every single ATP player has contributed to the world of tennis and its history just by being here and by putting in the work every single day,” she added.

Eala’s growing popularity has not gone unnoticed, earning recognition from fellow tennis stars and former US Davis Cup captain Patrick McEnroe. Even the US Open organizers made their move, assigning the charming left-hander to Louis Armstrong Stadium for her first-round match.
McEnroe previously urged that it would be "a great story" if the host put Eala on bigger courts
It is the second-largest court at the USTA Billie Jean King National Tennis Center as it can cater more than 14,000 spectators, behind the Arthur Ashe Stadium which accommodates nearly 24,000 fans.

There, the Southeast Asian Games champion faces American qualifier Mary Stoiana on Wednesday, Sept. 2 (Philippine time), marking their second showdown as they battled before in a W100 event in Landisville, Pennsylvania, where the former prevailed in straight sets.
Eala's appearance at Armstrong is expected to become a sold-out venue with most of the crowd being Filipinos.
Also, Eala drew cheers on the center court after competing in the Stars of the Open – an exhibition event – where she eventually bowed to her American friend Iva Jovic.

It turned out the most viewed match in U.S. Open's YouTube channel as it closing in on 2 million views, eclipsing the 2009 men's finals clash of Swiss tennis icon Roger Federer and Argentine Juan Martin del Potro.

But it can be recalled, Eala was already a big hit in the US Open last year, entering as a debutant in the main draw and making it a fitting one after she stunned 14th-ranked Clara Tauson, 6-3, 2-6, 7-6 (11), before the 8,000 spectators at the Grandstand.
Currently world No. 18 and 17th seed in the final major, Eala admitted that she is taking inspiration from her loved ones and country, helping her to continue to work on her unprecedented dreams.

“I would say, anything is possible and to dream big,” said Eala. “I think me as a person, I'm very ambitious, and although there was no one from my country who did this before, was successful in tennis, you know, I took inspiration from anyone I could, from my family, from my brother.”
“So I think just to be ambitious and to dream big and know that you can do it,” she added.
As she eyes another historic triumph in New York, Eala is also gearing up for her much-awaited appearance in the coming 2026 Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games in Japan.

articles.title: Summit Point returns to PGT spotlight, ready to test Tour’s best
articles.summary: Nine years after last hosting a Philippine Golf Tour championship, Summit Point Golf and Country Club makes a much-anticipated return to the PGT calendar, ready to once again put the country’s top…

blocks.text: Nine years after last hosting a Philippine Golf Tour championship, Summit Point Golf and Country Club makes a much-anticipated return to the PGT calendar, ready to once again put the country’s top professionals through one of the tour’s most demanding tests.

The ICTSI Summit Point Championship blasts off Sept. 8-11 in Lipa City, Batangas, with the Robert Trent Jones II-designed layout expected to challenge the men and ladies of the PGT with its combination of length, strategy and precision.

Clyde Mondilla ruled the last PGT event staged at Summit Point – the ICTSI Players Championship – and went on to capture the 2017 PGT Order of Merit crown. Now, nearly a decade later, the course returns to the spotlight with another strong field eager to make its mark on a layout that rewards aggression off the tee but demands discipline from start to finish.

Known as the country’s first “tribute” course, Summit Point features holes modeled after renowned layouts and signature holes from famous international courses. But while its design pays homage to golf landmarks around the world, it has developed a character and set of challenges all its own.

At 7,017 yards, the course gives the long hitters plenty of opportunities to attack, but power alone will not be enough to conquer it. Recent monsoon rains have softened the fairways, potentially narrowing the advantage of the biggest hitters. Strong winds are also expected to add another layer of difficulty.

The mix of short, strategic holes and long, demanding par-4s and par-5s will require players to make sound decisions throughout the four rounds. Large bunkers, water hazards and ravines stand ready to punish errant shots, while precise approach play and a dependable short game could prove decisive.
The four par-3s could also emerge as pivotal holes in the championship. With little room for error, they offer opportunities to gain ground – or quickly derail a title bid.

Reigning Order of Merit champion Angelo Que and Mondilla are expected to banner the field in the P2.5 million championship, the fifth leg of the 10-stage circuit organized by Pilipinas Golf Tournaments, Inc.

The event comes after a lengthy two-month break in the PGT calendar, with the last two legs played in July. Lloyd Go swept those final two stops, prevailing in contrasting fashion at the tight, undulating Pinewoods course in Baguio before edging Tony Lascuña by one stroke at the flat and wide Pradera Verde in Pampanga.

The extended break should leave the field both rested and hungry, giving the pros – including those competing in the accompanying 54-hole, P1 million Ladies PGT – more time to sharpen their games and prepare for the second half of the season. Several players have also seen action in overseas tournaments during the hiatus, adding another intriguing element to the battle at Summit Point.
But much of the attention will inevitably center on the course itself.

Summit Point's return to the PGT stage provides a distinctly different challenge from the tour's recent stops. It invites players to unleash their power, yet punishes indiscriminate aggression. The softened fairways could encourage more attacking lines, but the hazards, ravines and demanding approach shots will require players to know when to push and when to play conservatively.

After nine years away, Summit Point is back – and it is poised to make the PGT's return a test of not just who can hit it farthest, but who can manage the course, withstand the conditions and remain patient over four demanding days.

articles.title: 3 transformative leaders named 2026 Ramon Magsaysay Awardees
articles.summary: The Ramon Magsaysay Award Foundation on Monday, Aug. 31, named three individuals from Singapore, Bangladesh, and Myanmar as its 2026 awardees, recognizing their work in international diplomacy,…

blocks.text: The Ramon Magsaysay Award Foundation on Monday, Aug. 31, named three individuals from Singapore, Bangladesh, and Myanmar as its 2026 awardees, recognizing their work in international diplomacy, essential services for remote communities, and the fight for political prisoners’ rights.
The awardees are Singaporean statesman and diplomat Tommy Koh, Bangladeshi social development leader Runa Khan, and Myanmar human rights advocate Bo Kyi.
The announcement coincided with the 119th birth anniversary of former president Magsaysay, after whom the prestigious award was named.

“Our long line of Ramon Magsaysay awardees includes diplomats, statesmen, and public servants who have helped nations find common ground, strengthened international cooperation, and advanced the principles of international law,” the foundation said.
Diplomatic leadership
Koh was recognized for a career spanning more than six decades in diplomacy, international law, education, and institution-building.
He played a role in negotiations for the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea and helped countries with competing interests reach common ground.

His work in Singapore also extended to arts, culture, and heritage. He helped establish the Institute of Policy Studies, the Center for International Law, and Tembusu College at the National University of Singapore.
“Building a nation is not only about building institutions. It is also about shaping the people and ideas that give a country its character,” the foundation said.
Koh has also mentored generations of students, diplomats, scholars, public servants, and artists.
“At the heart of his work is a vocation that has remained constant through the many roles he has taken on: that of a teacher,” the foundation said.
The foundation said his influence is reflected in the people he has taught and mentored.

“But perhaps the clearest measure of Tommy Koh's life is not the number of institutions he helped build or agreements he helped shape. It is the people who came away from knowing a little more, thinking a little differently, or believing they could do a little more themselves,” it said.
“Tommy Koh embodies the Ramon Magsaysay ideal of greatness of spirit,” the foundation said.
Reaching communities
Khan was recognized for bringing healthcare and other essential services to communities in Bangladesh that are difficult to reach because of their location.
Her work began with a floating hospital that brought healthcare directly to communities along the country’s rivers.
It later grew into Friendship, the organization she founded, which expanded into education, livelihoods, and climate resilience.
“The challenge was not simply providing services. It was finding a way to bring them within reach of people who could not easily reach them,” the foundation said.
Khan eventually saw that the needs of these communities extended beyond healthcare.
“Healthcare was tied to education. Livelihoods were tied to resilience and communities facing a changing climate needed more than a single intervention,” the foundation said.
From the floating hospital grew Friendship’s broader work with communities.

“What began in the bodies of water became something much larger: a way of working that starts by listening, stays close to the people it serves and recognizes that every community has the knowledge and capacity to shape its own future,” the foundation said.
The foundation said Khan’s approach recognizes that communities themselves have the knowledge and capacity to shape their future.
“It means to reach someone not simply to bring a service closer to make sure that distance never takes away their dignity,” it said.
Remembering prisoners
Bo Kyi was recognized for decades of documenting political imprisonment in Myanmar and supporting political prisoners and their families.
A student activist during Myanmar’s 1988 democracy movement, he was imprisoned for his political beliefs. After his release, he continued working for those who remained behind bars.
In 2000, he helped establish the Assistance Association of Political Prisoners, which documented political imprisonment and supported the families of political prisoners.
“When he was released, he chose not to leave behind those who were still inside,” the foundation said.
For years, Bo Kyi has documented the experiences of political prisoners and kept their stories before the public.

“His words reminds us that imprisonment doesn't end with the person inside the cell. It reaches everyone waiting outside, and sometimes, what people need most is simply to know that someone remembers,” the foundation said.
“Bo Kyi has spent his life being that person,” it added.
The foundation said his work reflects the importance of keeping hope alive for people whose freedom has been taken away.
“And perhaps that is where freedom begins. Not when the locks turn, but when we refuse to accept that the locked door is the end of someone's story,” it said.

articles.title: Icac lawyer tells Charles Perrottet the key to lying is ‘you have to be really good at remembering it’
articles.summary: Perrottet disagrees when counsel assisting Peggy Dwyer SC claims brother of former NSW premier is not truthful and ‘constructing evidence’

blocks.text: A brother of former New South Wales premier Dominic Perrottet has told Icac he would lie to a property developer about delivering political outcomes “to keep him on side”, but Charles Perrottet has denied lying to the state’s anti-corruption watchdog.

Charles Perrottet, who is among three Liberal figures alleged to have anticipated receiving $2m in prohibited political donations from Jean Nassif, told the Independent Commission Against Corruption (Icac) on Monday that he “made up” updates for the property developer.

Perrottet said he provided advice with a “political flavour” when chasing payments for genuine services provided to Nassif’s company, Toplace, by lobbying company Beckington, which was controlled by Christian Ellis and Jeremy Greenwood, also named in Icac’s allegations.
Dominic Perrottet is not named as a person of interest nor is he accused of wrongdoing.

Charles Perrottet, a member of the NSW Liberals’ conservative right faction, said he advised Nassif in the hope the developer would a sign a statutory declaration about allegations that the rival centre-right faction was circumventing electoral funding laws which prevent property developers from donating.
Under questioning from counsel assisting, Peggy Dwyer SC, he rejected the suggestion that his arrangement with Nassif was similar to the one he sought to expose.
“So you were doing that by promising Jean Nassif that you could achieve political outcomes for him if he gave money, correct?” Dwyer asked on Monday.
Perrottet replied: “They’re very separate issues.” He has insisted payments from Nassif were not political donations.

Dwyer read a message about the allegations against the centre-right – for which the commission heard Nassif never provided a statutory declaration – that Charles Perrottet sent to Ellis in February 2020: “It’s the money train. They cannot donate, but they get around that in two ways: cash and monthly government affairs retainers … the going rate is $50,000 per month.”
Dwyer suggested that Perrottet had been trying to set up “the same sort of arrangement to help the right”.
“You wanted to get on board the money train, didn’t you?” she said. Charles Perrottet denied this.

Earlier on Monday, Charles Perrottet was asked about a message he sent to Nassif in January 2021, in which he provided a “short summary” on actions he had taken in relation to three Toplace developments, including the reference “189 spoke to my PDU contact”.
The commission heard that “189” referred to a Toplace development in Parramatta and “PDU” referred to the NSW Planning Delivery Unit. Perrottet said he did not have a PDU contact and made no call.

“Ultimately, I made it up,” Perrottet told the Icac hearing. He said under questioning he would lie to Nassif by “regularly mislead[ing]” him about his own involvement in lobbying work by Beckington for Toplace.

“At times, I would add my own political flavour to it to keep him on side,” he said. He said this included “many messages of me providing political updates to encourage him to make those payments [to Beckington]”.

He was asked about at a meeting he attended at a Sydney pub in January 2021 with Toplace executive Sharangan Maheswaran, named in another of Icac’s allegations, at which messages suggested Charles Perrottet had collected a cheque for $148,500 for Beckington.
Charles Perrottet accepted he had told Nassif the money was for “assistance for the upcoming preselections”, but told the commission it was in fact for genuine lobbying work by Beckington.

blocks.caption: Property developer Jean Nassif, who fled Australia in 2022, is expected to appear befoer Icac via video link from Lebanon on Friday. Photograph: PR IMAGE

blocks.text: After Dwyer said his evidence contradicted a private examination in June in which he said he was there to pick up Nassif’s statutory declaration, Charles Perrottet said: “It could be both.” Dwyer accused him of lying to the commission.
after newsletter promotion
“The great truism about telling a lie, Mr Perrottet, is you have to be really good at remembering it,” she said.

“And when you gave evidence in June this year that you were picking up a statutory declaration that was a lie, and when you gave evidence this morning that you didn’t know what you were picking up, that was a lie.
“And you, when confronted with the truth about it being a cheque, you’re constructing your evidence around that. That’s what’s going on here.”
Charles Perrottet said: “I disagree.”
The commission heard evidence about an arrangement under which Beckington would receive 1% of the total Nassif made from any developments they were successful in fast-tracking.
“His example of the 1% for any project that could get through, and he gave an example of if you made $100m, you’d get 1%,” Charles Perrottet said.

Perrottet repeatedly insisted that he provided “advice”, rather than work, to Nassif. Perrottet told the inquiry he had agreed that his wife, Anita Perrottet, would receive money for advice he provided to Nassif through her business Macquarie Consulting from Beckington, controlled by Ellis and Greenwood, and JPG Advisory, controlled by Greenwood.
The watchdog has evidence the payments to Anita Perrottet totalled $660,999 over two-and-half years. She has told the commission this was for “stragetic and marketing advice” she provided.
Under questioning from the presiding commissioner, Fabian Gleeson, Charles Perrottet said it was his understanding at the time that this was not income he had to disclose in his tax return.

He said he had met with Ellis and Anita to discuss the invoice arrangement, but Dwyer said this directly contradicted Anita Perrottet’s evidence to the commission last week, in which she said she had only spoken with Greenwood about payments.
“My recollection is the invoicing conversations that I had, and I believe Anita was present, were with Christian,” Charles Perrottet said.
Nassif, who fled Australia in 2022, is expected to appear by video link from Lebanon on Friday. He has previously denied any wrongdoing.
Icac’s inquiry continues.

articles.title: UST, FEU reign supreme in Intercol Div 1
articles.summary: Reigning UAAP champions University of Santo Tomas and Far Eastern University capped an action-packed 2026 PTTF Intercollegiate and Interscholastic Challenge by claiming the Men’s and Women’s Division…

blocks.text: Reigning UAAP champions University of Santo Tomas and Far Eastern University capped an action-packed 2026 PTTF Intercollegiate and Interscholastic Challenge by claiming the Men’s and Women’s Division 1 titles, respectively, on Sunday, Aug. 30, at the Home Court at Ayala Malls Manila Bay in Parañaque City.

It was a 1–2 finish for the reigning six-peat men’s champions, with UST-1, featuring reigning UAAP MVP Abraham Antivo IV, multiple-time UAAP High School Boys’ MVP Jebb Datahan, and Season 86 Rookie of the Year Josh Manlapaz, taking the title over UST-2’s Josh Aguilar, Al-J Sanchez, Alvin Sevilla, and Aljay Villena.

“Sobrang laking bagay 'to sa 'min kasi dito namin nate-test yung skills namin papatating nga sa UAAP. Masaya naman (aa performance) kasi nailabas rin po namin yung karo namin,” said Antivo, who highlighted the tournament’s value as preparation for the UAAP.

The tournament was backed by the Huaching Foundation, Philippine Sports Commission, PLDT, Topcoms Marketing Inc.—the authorized distributor of Mizuno Philippines—Cara Celine Dormtel, Gold Cross Security Agency, and Best Options Assistance Inc., along with Dino Jalandoni, Bombit Silva, and Eric Ongkauco.

On the women’s side, FEU-1 also secured the championship in two matches, with Shy Gabisay and Christine Golez defeating De La Salle College of Saint Benilde’s Zachi Chua and Gytha Valdez, 6–11, 11–6, 11–9, 11–3, in the doubles match.
Last UAAP season’s MVP Chrishien Santillan earlier defeated her NCAA counterpart Jesmaine Tayag, 11–5, 11–5, 11–7, to put FEU on the cusp of the championship.

“Malaking bagay sa exposure po talaga, at the same time ma-figure out din po namin ang magiging lineup sa UAAP. Tsaka mga kailangan naming i- na weaknesses namin,” said Santillan, who was also a former NCAA MVP.

The two Tiger Paddlers squads dominated their respective Katipunan foes in the semifinals. UST-1 swept University of the Philippines-2 in two matches, 3–2 and 3–1, while UST-2 also defeated UP-2 in two matches, 3–0 and 3–1.
Meanwhile, FEU-1 took down Blue Paddlers-1 in two matches, 3–1 and 3–0, while CSB stopped the Angel Laude-led DLSU-1 in both matches, 3–2, to arrange the championship showdown.

Over in Division 2, UST-3 completed its dominant run by sweeping Rizal Technological University-2, 3–0 and 3–0, to claim the men’s title, while University of Mindanao-3 captured the women’s championship over UP-2.
UST-3’s men’s team was composed of Dirk Atilano, Josh Canalin, Louise Gacias, and Laurence Melendez, while UM-3 fielded Ayesha Quibol, Charlotte Delos Reyes, and Jennylee Dable.
UST-5, featuring high school boys’ singles champion Emmanuel Paculba alongside Josh Banas and Franz Acasio, won the high school boys’ team title.
National Academy of Sports-1, meanwhile, claimed the high school girls’ championship over NAS-2.

articles.title: Newborn baby’s body found in Sydney rubbish bin as police hold ‘serious concerns’ for mother
articles.summary: Police urge mother to attend hospital after baby’s body discovered in Harrow Road in Auburn

blocks.text: New South Wales police have appealed for information to find the mother of a newborn baby boy, whose body was discovered in a rubbish bin in Auburn in Sydney’s south-west on Monday morning.

Police said emergency services responded to reports of the body of a baby located in a rubbish bin along Harrow Road in Auburn at 11.20am, with officers from the Auburn police area command finding the body of a newborn boy.
A crime scene has been established and detectives have commenced an investigation into the incident.
Police said they hold “serious concerns” for the welfare of the baby’s mother, and have urged the mother to attend the nearest hospital to receive urgent care.

Anyone with more information about the incident, or who was in the area at the time and may have dashcam or mobile footage relevant to the incident, are urged to contact Auburn police station or Crime Stoppers on 1800 333 000.
Police were due to hold a press conference on the matter at 4pm AEST.
More to come

articles.title: Kenyan runners stamp class in Pru Life UK run
articles.summary: Kenyans Gilbert Muge and Pamela Bundotich flashed a potent combination of speed and endurance, weathering dark skies and intermittent drizzle to stamp their class in the centerpiece 30-km race of the…

blocks.text: Kenyans Gilbert Muge and Pamela Bundotich flashed a potent combination of speed and endurance, weathering dark skies and intermittent drizzle to stamp their class in the centerpiece 30-km race of the Pru Life UK POP (Promise of Protection) Run at the Ayala Triangle Gardens in Makati last Sunday, Aug. 30.

Muge and Bundotich wasted little time flexing the racing form honed through numerous international competitions, pulling away from a field of Filipino challengers and adding another pair of victories to their growing list of triumphs on local roads.
Muge, whose most recent victory on Philippine soil came in the Trilogy Run Asia 2026 in March, seized control early and never looked back, clocking 1:44:03 in the novel 30K distance.
James Cruz finished six minutes behind Muge in 1:50:44, while Aldrin Serrano clocked 2:01:31 for third.

The 30K race was one of five categories offered in the event, which sought to cater to runners across the spectrum – from beginners taking their first steps into the sport to seasoned athletes looking for a demanding new milestone.

The distance also carried special significance for Pru Life UK, which created the 30km race to mark its 30 years in the Philippines. Rather than simply adding another race category, the company positioned the 30 kilometers as a physical representation of its three decades of serving Filipino policyholders and communities.
Bundotich, a familiar presence in various regional marathon events in the country, likewise proved too strong for the local field, topping the women's 30km in 2:02:38.
Tricia Rufano came in second in 2:17:32, while Edna Magtubo was third in 2:26:02.
The other titles disputed were in the 3K, 5K, 10K and 21K categories, producing several close finishes in the race organized by Sunrise Events, Inc.
National athlete Jessa Mae Roda captured the women's 21K crown in 1:29:49, beating Nicole Diloy, who clocked 1:33:26. Fayelle Castro finished third in 2:01:43.
Roy Laudit, meanwhile, ruled the men's 21K in 1:16:03, turning back Ricky Organiza, who finished in 1:19:19. Kenyan Evans Bomer was a close third in 1:19:21.

Alfred Braza emerged on top in a tightly contested men's 10K, clocking 32:43 to beat Junel Gobotia (33:13) and Noli Torre (33:43), while Meljoy Gonzales took the women's 10K crown in 40:29, holding off Kenyan Purity Serem, who finished in 41:31. Angel Lumacang was third in 42:53.

The men's 5K produced one of the day's closest finishes, with Jevie Rebutazo edging Rahby Seno by just one second. Rebutazo clocked 16:21, while Seno settled for second in 16:22. Matthew Donnery was third in 17:08.
The women's 5K was likewise decided by a matter of seconds, with Kaye Villanueva timing 19:17 to beat Princess Amarante, who clocked 19:36. Nila Acampado finished third in 21:17.
Jerico Cadag and Marilou Caduyac completed the 3K sweep, winning the men's and women's divisions in 9:22 and 11:24, respectively.

Joe Ross Simangan was second in the men's 3K in 9:47, while Gian Clava placed third in 10:23. In the women's race, Yessamin Carbonilla clocked 12:17 for second, followed by Maria Lyn Balguma in 15:17.

articles.title: Monday briefing: Nepal and Tibet’s floods are a warning for the future
articles.summary:
In today’s newsletter: As rescuers search for survivors after catastrophic floods, the disaster offers a stark warning about the climate risks facing the region, and the world

Good morning.…

blocks.text: Good morning. Over the weekend, rescue workers in Nepal and Tibet raced to find people who are still trapped in villages affected by catastrophic flash floods. As of this morning, the death toll stands at 903, and more than 4,000 people are missing.

For those of you reading this in a place where life continues as usual, the scale of devastation is hard to fathom. In a matter of minutes, a torrent of mud and debris engulfed entire villages, snapped bridges and swept away people’s homes and families. Some survivors are marooned on top of buildings that rescue workers can’t reach. Others are trapped in tunnels beneath the ground. Many have no idea if their loved ones are still alive.

The floods exemplify a wider threat. The delicate processes that have shaped our climate for centuries are unwinding at a terrifying pace. Scientists are still investigating the precise sequence of events that caused these floods, but as the planet heats up and glaciers melt, events like this will keep happening.

The Guardian has been covering the floods extensively – you can read our visual guide to the disaster, and our latest report on it here. For this morning’s newsletter, I spoke to our south Asia correspondent Hannah Ellis-Petersen, who is on the ground in Kathmandu. She’s been speaking to survivors and reporting on the rescue operation since Thursday. That’s after the headlines.
Weekend roundup

items: UK politics | PC Andrew Harper’s killers will remain in prison after Andy Burnham announced changes to the early release scheme that will see anyone convicted of unlawful killing, including all forms of manslaughter, excluded from the scheme.

Milo Yiannopoulos | Far-right British media provocateur Milo Yiannopoulos has been deported from the US back to the UK by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) in connection with what the agency said was expired authorisation to be in the country.

US-Iran | Iran has launched retaliatory strikes on airbases in Jordan after the United States attacked Iranian rocket launchers on an island in the strait of Hormuz, the first such strikes in a month.
Iceland | In a blow to Brussels, Iceland has held a referendum that has narrowly ⁠rejected ⁠the government’s proposal ​to hold ⁠accession talks with ⁠the ​EU.

Nepal-Tibet disaster | A headteacher in Nepal evacuated 900 children from a school moments before a deadly wall of water struck their town amid the devastating flash floods that have killed almost 800 people and left thousands missing.

blocks.text: In depth: An ‘absolute catastrophe’

blocks.caption: ‘Everything was either submerged in mud, or mangled’  Photograph: cnsphoto/Reuters

blocks.text: At 8:37am on Wednesday morning, an enormous chunk of ice from a glacier in the Himalayas broke off and crashed on to a mountain near the border between Nepal and Tibet. It caused a fearsome avalanche of ice and rock, which surged downstream into the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers, submerging villages and sweeping roads away.

At first, the scale of damage was unclear. Nepal is prone to natural disasters, and many of the villages affected by these floods are extremely remote. Early satellite images of the region were obscured by thick clouds of dust, and scientists initially assumed that an earthquake must have caused the flood, rather than a glacier collapse. By Wednesday night, as more images and reports emerged, it became clear that the floods were an “absolute catastrophe,” Hannah says. On Thursday, she boarded a flight to Kathmandu, the capital city near the destruction.

When Hannah arrived in Bidur, a small city two hours from Kathmandu, on Friday morning, most of its buildings had been destroyed, their carcasses exposed like matchsticks. A team of rescue workers in yellow hard hats were working to clear the roads. “There was a bank, an ATM machine, and a truck that was lying on its side,” she says. “Everything else was either submerged in mud, or mangled.”
The race to save lives

The Nepali army has been organising the rescue operation from a military base in Bidur. Large sections of the road that links Bidur to villages higher in the valley have been washed away, so rescues are happening by air, and the sound of helicopters is nearly constant. Every two to three minutes, a chopper lands, deposits survivors, and sets off again. The mud is so thick in some places that helicopters have struggled to land. Rasuwa, an area where entire villages were destroyed, was still inaccessible when I spoke to Hannah on Sunday afternoon. “The ground zero of the floods has still not been reached by journalists, and is only just being reached by the army,” she says.

Hundreds, if not thousands, of people have been rescued, and hundreds of people are now waiting outside the army base in Bidur scanning lists of survivors posted on the walls. At hospitals in Kathmandu, health workers have put up photos of bodies that are so disfigured their families have struggled to identify them. Authorities have begun burying human remains because there isn’t enough mortuary space to prevent them from decomposing. “I’ve spoken to people who have up to 12 relatives who have gone missing,” says Hannah, who visited hospitals in Kathmandu on Saturday. “And there’s no phone signal in the more remote villages. So another big cause of suffering is this huge uncertainty.”
Thousands still missing

So far there are 4,247 people who are missing, according to Nepal’s disaster agency (592 of whom are foreigners, including 43 Australians, and 48 from the UK, including 15 reported missing in China). Among them are 933 workers from Nepal and neighbouring countries who were working on hydroelectric power projects along the river. These rely on vast tunnel systems that are built deep into the ground, and rescue teams have to dig through mud and bore through tunnel walls to extricate trapped workers. On Saturday, the Nepali army had a small breakthrough when it successfully inserted a pipe into a tunnel at a hydroelectric site in Trishuli, allowing air to be pumped into the tunnel. In the early hours this morning, rescue efforts were “intensified” at the site, with a team of 90 people deployed.

The army is racing against time to rescue the living. “People are stuck in areas that have no drinking water, or access to food. They’re completely cut off,” Hannah says. The picture of devastation has emerged more quickly in Nepal than in Tibet, where the Chinese government retains a tight grip on information. On Friday, as the official death toll in Nepal rose to 538 people, China estimated that just five people had died in Tibet. The Chinese authorities have since revised their numbers, and estimate that at least 16 people are dead and 546 missing.
The long road to recovery

It will take months to clear away the mud, and some people will never find their relatives’ bodies. Some were pushed so far down the river that they have washed up in India. “People have lost everything,” says Hannah. “I saw one woman clutching a bottle of cooking oil, because it’s the only thing she had left.” Climate stories in the global south often struggle to break through, so it’s encouraging that these floods have been covered so widely. But when the news cycle has moved on, Nepal will be left with the enormous task of rebuilding. It estimates that cost could be between $4bn to $5bn, almost a tenth of its economy.

“It’s getting increasingly difficult for Nepal to pick itself up,” Hannah tells me. In Kathmandu, buildings destroyed by the 2015 earthquake, which killed nearly 9,000 people, are still in ruins. The EU has committed €2m to Nepal to help with the floods, and Britain has committed £5m. There’s also been a lot of focus on the need for better early monitoring systems. All of this matters. But as Sunil Acharya, a climate policy specialist based in Kathmandu, wrote in this interesting Opinion column, it also obscures a more fundamental problem: systems to monitor these events were designed for yesterday’s risks, not today’s extremes. Nepal’s warning systems were destroyed before they could alert people near the source of the flood.

Looming over all this is the fact that nations like Nepal, which has contributed a minuscule amount to historic greenhouse gas emissions, will suffer the worst effects of the climate crisis. It needs far more assistance to cope with the consequences of richer nations’ actions. And it needs those nations to rapidly cut their emissions, before the crisis gets worse.
The week to come

items: Tuesday | Justice secretary Alex Norris is due to present the government’s revised plans for the prisoner early release scheme, which includes a headroom review aimed at freeing up more space in the system.
Thursday | In the first UK visit by an EU leader of Andy Burnham’s tenure, the prime minister is will host talks with French president Emmanuel Macron.

Saturday | Officials from Jamaica will visit the UK to lodge a petition with King Charles to seek legal guidance from the privy council on the country’s request for reparations over Britain’s involvement in the slave trade, on the anniversary of the 1781 Zong slave ship departure from West Africa.

The front pages

The Times writes “Early release blocked for manslaughter prisoners”, while the Mail’s take is “More dangerous criminals set to be freed early”, and the Telegraph says “Burnham to free high-risk criminals”.

The i Paper splashes “Harry should pay for security costs in UK, say two-thirds of public in poll”, the Express leads with “‘I fear Andrew’s staff won’t co-operate with police’”, and the FT has “Big Tech profits enjoy $160bn paper boost from stakes in other AI groups”. The Sun’s headline is “United for dad”.

For decades, Eliezer Yudkowsky has been trying to warn the world about the dangers of AI. Now people are finally listening to him, but is it too late? Guardian journalist Michael Safi looks into the world of artificial intelligence, exploring the dangers and promises it holds for society.

blocks.text: The Upside
A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad

blocks.caption: The number of people living with dementia around the world is forecast to nearly triple to 153 million by 2050. Photograph: Joe Giddens/PA

blocks.text: Results from a 15-year study suggest that statins, the cholesterol-busting drugs, can lower the risk of dementia by 15%. In the largest study of its kind, researchers tracked more than 132,000 people in Denmark between 2006 and 2021. Those who started on statins during the study period were 10% less likely to develop dementia. Those taking them early reduced their risk by 15%. The results were similar in women and men. The number of people living with dementia globally is forecast to nearly triple to 153 million by 2050. But, experts believe almost half of dementia cases could be prevented or delayed.

blocks.text: Magkakakabit na problema ang edukasyon, kahirapan, at hanapbuhay — at sa kaso ng Pilipinas, perpetuating cycle ito ng underdevelopment

items: The Philippines has achieved a single-digit poverty rate of 9.7% in 2025, the lowest in history, but the Multidimensional Poverty Index indicates that 12.8% of the population remains multidimensionally poor.

Despite being classified as an upper-middle-income country with a GNI per capita of $4,850, significant income disparities exist across regions, with average incomes varying greatly between areas like Makati and Zamboanga.

The country faces a severe literacy crisis, with 88% of students unable to read at a Grade 7 level, which poses challenges for future employment and perpetuates a cycle of poverty and underdevelopment.

Nag-single-digit poverty rate na pala ang Pilipinas? Ayon sa datos ng Philippine Statistics Authority, 9.7% na lang and mahihirap na Pilipino noong 2025, ang pinakamababa sa kasaysayan. Katumbas nito ang 11.08 milyong Pilipino, mula sa 17.54 milyon noong 2023. ‘Yan ang statistic No. 1 natin.

blocks.caption: AnimatEd,Editorial, Poverty, Flooding, Money

blocks.text: Pero mismong bagong datos ng gobyerno ang nagsasabing baka hindi ito totoo kapag tiningnan sa lente ng edukasyon, pabahay at batayang serbisyo, kalusugan, at hanapbuhay. Ayon sa Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) — nasa double digit pa rin o 12.8% ang multidimensionally poor. ‘Yan ang statistic No. 2.
May tatlo pang datos na dapat ibangga riyan kapag tiningnan natin ang kahirapan sa Pilipinas.

Statistic No. 3, sa wakas classified na tayo na upper-middle income country, na may GNI [gross national income] per capita of $4,850 (mahigit-kumulang P291,000 sa palitang $1 = P60). At disclaimer ng mga economist, hindi ito ang be-all and end-all. Yugto lang daw ito sa development journey.
Ang GNI per capita kas ay isang average statistic. Hindi nito ipinapakita ang disparity o agwat sa kinikita ng mayaman at mahirap.

At karugtong niyan ang statistic No. 4, na nagsasabing malala pa rin ang income disparities across regions, ayon sa latest Family Income and Expenditure Survey (FIES) ng Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA). Ibig sabihin, may Luzon-Mindanao divide pagdating sa income ng mga pamilyang Pilipino.
Halimbawa, habang nasa P796,990 ang average income sa Makati, sa Zamboanga’y kakarampot na P309,610.

Lumago raw ang income ng mga pamilyang Pilipino nang 16.5% mula 2023 hanggang 2025, pero lumobo rin ang spending na umabot sa 24.7%. Kaya hindi natin naramdamang may extra income tayo, dahil ubos lakas sa gastusin.

Ang average annual family income ng Pilipino ay P411,350 ayon sa FIES. Malaki sana, pero kapag tiningnan mo in dollars, $6,610 lamang ‘yan. For comparison sa pinakamayamang bansa sa Southeast Asia na Singapore, ang average annual household income nito ay approximately US$149,000 (P8,940,000) habang US$9,970 (P698,200) naman ang sa Vietnam, ang sinusundan ng Pilipinas sa listahan.
Sabi ng mga yumamang galing sa hirap, “hindi balakid sa tagumpay ang kahirapan.” We salute you, kayong lahat na nagsikap at nakaahon sa hirap.
Pero para sa karaniwang Pilipino, paano ka makaaahon sa hirap kung palyado ang educational system na kinalakhan mo?

At diyan pumapasok ang statistic No. 5: Ayon sa Final Report ng EDCOM 2, “severe” ang literacy crisis sa bansa, kung saan 88% ng mag-aaral ay hindi nakababasa sa Grade 7 level at 0.4% lamang ang proficient pag tapak ng Grade 12. (BASAHIN: 88% of students entering Grade 7 struggling to read at that level)

Ito ang krisis na nakaamba sa Pilipinas — sa kabila ng pag-angat ngayong 2026, masu-sustain ba ito? Kapag sumali na sa labor force ang mga kabataang mababa ang kalidad ng edukasyon, paano sila matatanggap kung wala sa kanila ang skills na hinahanap ng employers? At siyempre, mauuwi ‘yan sa paglala ng unemployment at underemployment. Saan tayo pupulutin bilang bansa?
Magkakakabit na problema ang edukasyon, kahirapan, at hanapbuhay — at sa kaso ng Pilipinas, perpetuating cycle ito ng underdevelopment.

Kung ipinanganak kang mahirap, dehado kang makaangat dahil wala kang access sa kalidad na edukasyon. Maaaring lugmok ka sa kultura ng kahirapang nagdudulot ng helplessness at inferiority complex. Malamang din, tingin mo sa politiko ay padrinong pagkukunan ng ayuda, hindi tagapagsulong ng opportunity equality.

At ‘yan ang cycle na kailangang maigpawan, upang magkaroon ng tunay na pagkakataon ang mahihirap na makaangat sa buhay. ‘Yan ang delubyong tila umaanod sa ating papalayo sa panaginip nating maginhawang buhay. – Rappler.com
