articles.title: Iran supreme leader calls for unity among Muslim countries
articles.summary: TEHRAN — Iran’s supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei on Sunday called on Muslim countries in the region to unite against the United States and Israel, in a written message issued six months on…

blocks.text: TEHRAN — Iran’s supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei on Sunday called on Muslim countries in the region to unite against the United States and Israel, in a written message issued six months on from the start of the Middle East war.

Khamenei, in power since shortly after his father Ali Khamenei was killed at the start of the war on February 28, has yet to be seen in public since his appointment, and authorities have not released any video or audio of him.

“The solution to the problems of the Islamic nations is unity of words, friendship, and cooperation on the path of goodness,” he said Sunday as Shia Muslims marked the birthday of the Prophet Mohammed.

“Anyone, in any position, who does anything that leads to division among Muslims and creates conflict in the Muslim community, knowingly or unknowingly, intentionally or unintentionally, has served the purpose of the enemies of Islam,” he added, according to his official website.
The supreme leader called on the rulers of regional countries to “recognise your real enemy, understand its plan, and confront it”, referring to the US and Israel.
During the war, Iran targeted US military bases across the Middle East including in Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Jordan, Kuwait, Qatar and Bahrain.
Relations with those nations have since soured.
Khamenei, who has the final say on major state policies, also called on Iranian officials and citizens to put aside differences and come together against Israel and the United States.
“Again, this servant’s advice to the Iranian people is to not allow any differences to arise among themselves in any way,” he said, echoing remarks made in another statement on Friday.
“I firmly declare that doing anything detrimental to social cohesion is prohibited,” he had said in Friday’s message.

He also called Friday for the gradual de-dollarization of the Iranian economy and for boosting economic production to support growth following months of a US naval blockade and years of crippling sanctions that have hit livelihoods. /dl

articles.title: Nepal’s high-tech disaster response meets low-tech reality
articles.summary: KATHMANDU — The floods in the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers have exposed a striking gap in the country’s emergency response. The government agencies are increasingly using digital portals,…

blocks.text: KATHMANDU — The floods in the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers have exposed a striking gap in the country’s emergency response. The government agencies are increasingly using digital portals, drones, GIS, satellite images and artificial intelligence to collect and share information, while rescuers on the ground still lack enough specialized equipment to reach people trapped under mud and debris.

State agencies, including the Prime Minister’s Office, Nepali Army, Nepal Police and the national disaster management authority (NDRRMA), have launched extensive information drives across social media platforms, emergency SMS broadcasts, mobile ringtone alerts, and specialised applications.

Concurrently, independent tech groups and civic initiatives have rolled out digital mapping tools, tracing scripts, and open-source data repositories to track missing individuals and compile disaster statistics.

Yet, as the death toll rises and survivors remain isolated, technical analysts, emergency responders, and affected citizens point out a stark contrast. While the country’s digital communication strategy appears polished, its physical search, rescue, and early warning infrastructure remains woefully underdeveloped.

On Saturday, a video circulated widely on social media showing a Nepali Army search team navigating the tunnel of the Trishuli Hydroelectric Project to locate trapped workers. The soldiers relied entirely on the small beams of their smartphone flashlights.

The video sparked immediate public outcry. “Without proper equipment, in the faint light of a mobile phone?” commented social media user Irsad Ansari. Many others echoed his disbelief, asking how complex subterranean rescue operations could succeed without specialized industrial lighting, heavy demolition tools, and advanced tunneling equipment.

Though the government has attempted to project a modern, ‘smart’ response through digital maps and online dashboards, critics argue that these efforts fail to translate into tangible assistance on the ground. Public frustration has mounted into a familiar refrain across affected communities: The government is active on social media, but absent in society; it lives in the cloud, but fails on the ground.

On paper, several tech-driven coordination systems have been activated. The Ministry of Home Affairs and NDRRMA, in collaboration with the Department of Roads, recently launched the ‘Setu Rapid’ portal. The platform aims to integrate field rescuers, regional command posts, and heavy equipment operators onto a single live map.

Similarly, the Prime Minister’s Office established an integrated emergency assistance portal to process rescue requests, log missing persons reports, and track relief supply distributions. Emergency communications are also being funneled through the National Emergency Operation Centre, the Flood Forecasting Division, and NDRRMA’s dedicated hotline (1234).

To streamline relief donations, the government has set up integrated QR code payments through platforms like Nepal Clearing House Limited (NCHL), ConnectIPS, eSewa, and major commercial banking applications. Authorities have urged the public to donate solely through official channels, warning against unverified QR codes circulating online.

Minister for Education, Science, Technology and Innovation Mahabir Pun defended the state’s technological strategy, assuring that the government is utilizing available digital tools to the fullest extent for search, rescue, and rebuilding.

“We are currently working alongside a dedicated team of young IT professionals and artificial intelligence specialists to collect and process critical damage data,” Pun said. “Our nation has never properly established an integrated early warning system. That neglect in the past is precisely why we are facing such immense destruction today. Moving forward, prioritizing early warning systems across all vulnerable river basins will be our absolute top duty.”

Security forces maintain that advanced rescue teams have been deployed to the affected zones. Netra Bahadur Karki, spokesperson for the Armed Police Force, stated that specialized personnel including live detection equipment operators, drone squads, rope rescue teams, swift-water divers, and collapsed-structure search teams are actively working in the field.
Nepali Army spokesperson Rajaram Basnet added that heavy physical breaching tools, such as demolition hammers, rotary hammers, and helicopter rescue baskets, are being utilized where feasible.

To assess the damage across devastated swathes of Rasuwa, Nuwakot, and Dhading districts, civil tech groups have stepped in to assist state agencies. Bikas Krochme Gurung, an engineer and president of the Robotics Association of Nepal, explained that his organization’s Drone Rapid Response Team is deploying aerial photography, thermal imaging, and LiDAR sensors to map devastated areas.

“Where landslides have completely washed away highways and bridges, drones have proven crucial for measuring the distance between severed riverbanks, assessing erosion depth, and analyzing mudflow density,” said Gurung. “We are sending geo-referenced data directly to the NDRRMA and the Ministry of Home Affairs to help prioritise immediate rescue missions. Currently, between 80 and 100 trained drone pilots are on standby across the country.”

According to Gurung, the Drone Federation of India and Indian security forces have offered to supply additional drone units. However, because low-altitude drone operations can interfere with air traffic, aerial drone missions are being strictly managed alongside emergency military helicopters, which are currently dedicated exclusively to airlifting trapped survivors rather than dropping relief supplies.

Despite these efforts, social media influencers and public commentators argue that the disaster has laid bare Nepal’s structural vulnerabilities. Popular social media influencer Victor Paudel noted that the country’s physical response mechanism relies heavily on manual labour.

blocks.caption: Specialised teams drill a rock in Trishuli on Saturday in search of a hydropower project tunnel to rescue people trapped inside, in Rasuwa. RSS

blocks.text: “This disaster has exposed our severe lack of modern emergency response technology,” Paudel said. “If we had deployed the advanced rescue systems used in countries like South Korea, India, or China, the search operations would be far further along. Those nations possess extensive technical expertise in rescuing workers trapped in underground coal mines, hydroelectric tunnels, and highway caverns.”

Paudel pointed out that while security personnel on the ground deserve praise for working tirelessly, seeing soldiers clearing tons of thick mud and retrieving bodies with their bare hands proves that Nepal lacks a resilient disaster management system.

The stark operational contrast is visible across the border. In neighboring China, advanced heavy-lift drones capable of carrying humans have been deployed during flood rescues. In Nepal, however, hydro-project workers remained trapped inside dark water tunnels for four consecutive days due to a total lack of subterranean breaching equipment.

“We still suffer from a critical lack of high-level technology and unified data,” Gurung said. “We do not possess specialised machinery to break into tunnels, nor do we have redundant emergency communication systems. Nationwide, we have only four or five drones capable of lifting payloads between 5 and 20 kilograms. In times like this, the vital importance of satellite internet and heavy rescue hardware becomes painfully obvious.”

Technical analysts also stress that the failure of early warning systems directly caused the heavy loss of life. Neither the Department of Hydrology and Meteorology nor NDRRMA managed to deliver timely, precise warnings to at-risk communities before floodwaters hit.

Analysts often point to the Koshi Barrage as a functional contrast, where continuous water-level telemetry stretching from the upper Koshi basin down to Barahakshetra allows authorities to issue timely warnings. Yet, such monitoring networks remain missing across the torrential rivers of central Nepal.

Rajib Subba, an IT expert and current Election Commissioner, warned that the proliferation of uncoordinated digital forms and competing web portals across various government ministries could backfire, leading to data duplication and operational confusion.

“Government teams are working hard with the limited tools they have, but systemic preparation should have happened long before,” Subba said. “Collecting data on missing persons must be handled strictly through a centralised, single-window system. When different agencies release separate forms and helpline numbers, coordination breaks down and vital information gets scattered.”
Subba, who previously worked on early warning studies for the volatile Tsho Rolpa glacial lake, questioned the sustainability of past investments.

“Why haven’t we installed 24-hour automated monitoring and warning systems along our most dangerous rivers?” he asked. “Despite massive funding from international donor agencies in the name of early warning systems, there is almost no lasting, practical impact on the ground.”

Unregulated settlement expansion and poorly engineered road construction along riverbanks have exacerbated the destruction. While mountain communities historically built homes on high, stable ridges, modern infrastructure has drawn settlements directly down to river margins.

“It is long past time we re-evaluated our entire approach to national development,” Subba said. “In this era of severe climate crisis, if we fail to deploy the right technology in the right places, we will never stop these recurring cycles of multi-billion-rupee destruction.”
Model example of AI use

Amid government shortcomings, private initiatives have attempted to fill the gap. Niraj Bhushal, an assistant IT officer at the Ministry of Finance, independently built the ‘Rasuwa-Bhote Koshi Flood Rescue Portal’. Hosted on GitHub and powered by Grok AI, the open-source platform has become a model for leveraging AI in emergency situations.

Bhushal’s portal automatically collects data every five minutes from official digital feeds published by the NDRRMA, Nepal Police, Nepali Army, and the Rasuwa District Administration Office. The AI model processes missing persons requests submitted via Google Forms, cross-referencing them against lists of rescued survivors to eliminate duplicates.
Furthermore, the system processes satellite imagery provided by the European Union’s UCOS, using AI to map structural damage such as collapsed bridges, buried houses, and blocked road segments.

“I built this portal independently, but I am now collaborating with young volunteers from the civic group Speak Up Nepal,” said Bhushal. “A non-resident Nepali in Australia, Shristi Mainali, provided $210 to power the system, while community chief at SpaceX AI, provided an additional $100 to ensure the servers stay online.”

Before any data is published on the portal, Grok AI assists in fact-checking and verifying the details. “The portal automatically compares missing persons reports with records of recovered individuals,” Bhushal explained. “For official PDF reports released by the Nepali Army and local authorities, I manually convert the data into CSV files before running them through the system.”

To protect citizens from fraudulent links, Bhushal linked his platform directly to official government portals. Clicking the ‘Rescue’ button redirects users to the Prime Minister’s emergency portal, while the ‘Donate’ button routes directly to the Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund.

“I work full-time at the Ministry of Finance during the day and devote my nights until 1-2am to updating this portal,” said Bhushal. “I created this so that panicked families wouldn’t have to search frantically across scattered websites during a crisis. AI has proven immensely effective in bringing clarity to this chaotic situation.” /dl

articles.title: Nepal floods: Indian, Chinese, Korean teams support rescue effort
articles.summary: KATHMANDU — The Nepali government, which was initially reluctant to accept various kinds of support offered by friendly nations, has started allowing them to carry out search and rescue…

blocks.text: KATHMANDU — The Nepali government, which was initially reluctant to accept various kinds of support offered by friendly nations, has started allowing them to carry out search and rescue operations for people trapped inside hydropower tunnels in the Trishuli basin.
On Saturday, three different teams from India, China and South Korea reached disaster-hit areas and hydropower projects in the search and rescue of stranded individuals.
An Indian team from the National Disaster Response Force that arrived in Kathmandu on Friday flew to Chilime and Langtang in coordination with the Nepali Army and the Armed Police Force.

A technical team from India carried out on-site reconnaissance of hydropower tunnels in the area affected by the flash flood, the Indian Embassy in Kathmandu stated. It would help facilitate early search and rescue of stranded individuals.
The 11-member Indian team was flown to the two designated areas but the Nepal government on Saturday turned down another Indian request to send a bigger search and rescue team.
Indian experts conducted a recce of tunnels in Chilime and Langtang power plants area with the Nepali Army, Indian Ambassador Naveen Srivastava wrote on X.

Kathmandu has been selective in accepting external assistance and decided to seek the support of foreign experts on tunnel rescue, DNA and forensic examination. As Nepal is looking for large-size freezers to manage bodies, the government is in close consultation with immediate neighbours and the international community, said Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal.

Writing on Facebook on Saturday, Prime Minister Balendra Shah said that the government has received 2,000 airtight bags each from India and China for managing bodies of victims. The government has requested 30 Bailey bridges with China, he stated.

As many foreign nationals are also missing, a dedicated Emergency Control Room has been established at the foreign ministry, Khanal told a news conference on Saturday. “Our diplomatic missions are also constantly sharing and updating verified information, and facilitating communication with families and extending any necessary assistance, identification and repatriation procedures.”
Hinting at why the government earlier did not accept foreign teams, the minister said Nepal’s security agencies and other response teams are currently handling the situation effectively.

“As operations continue, we have requested specific and specialised assistance from our friendly neighbours in areas where their support can further strengthen our search-and-rescue efforts such as opening the tunnels where people have been trapped,” Khanal said. Also useful would be technologies that help us locate people alive in the affected areas, quick forensic and DNA analysis and mortuaries.

On the question of why the government was reluctant to allow the foreign teams for search and rescue operations, Minister Khanal said Nepali security agencies are well familiar with the geography and terrain.
“Since the disaster struck in difficult terrain and narrow passes this time, the foreign teams may face difficulties flying over the affected areas.”
Only helicopters can fly in the narrow gorge, possibly only by Nepali pilots, he stressed. “Since the terrain is risky, we are sensitive to the safety of personnel deployed.”
An eleven-member specialised technical reconnaissance team for tunnel rescue from India has been mobilised and a tunnel rescue team from China has also arrived, he said.

The government has also allowed some South Korean experts to visit and inspect the disaster-hit areas. A team was moved on Saturday itself, said an official. Another team is seeking permission to deploy.
Soon after the disaster, South Korea had offered to conduct aerial surveys using drones to locate victims and rescue survivors but the Nepal government declined.
According to the Chinese Embassy, at the request of the Nepali government, China’s Ministry of Emergency Management urgently dispatched five tunnel experts to Nepal on Saturday.
The experts flew by helicopter from Kerung near the Chinese border to the disaster-hit areas in Nepal. They immediately joined the tunnel rescue operation at a hydropower station, the embassy stated.
In response to the needs of the rescue operation, another four Chinese tunnel experts will be urgently dispatched to Nepal soon, said the embassy.

On the modality of sharing of information between Nepal and China prior to a potential natural disaster, Minister Khanal said that the Tribhuvan University and the Chinese Academy of Science and Technology were working on it.
“After the disaster, we have had excellent coordination, communication and cooperation with China on sharing data and information,” said Khanal.

Prior to Wednesday’s floods, even the Chinese had no proper information about the looming disaster, Khanal said. There are no arrangements between the neighbours for the sharing of prior information. “We are in the process of having it,” said Khanal.
A six-member Chinese team landed in the Trishuli area by a Chinese helicopter. It will begin the rescue operation in close coordination with a Nepali Army team, according to statements.

Although the conditions inside the Trishuli 3 B tunnel in Rasuwa remain extremely challenging, the government of Nepal,the Nepali Army and Chinese expert team are making every possible effort, the PM’s Office stated.
Nepal and China have maintained close communication on transboundary disaster management, the Chinese Embassy in Kathmandu said in a public notice on Saturday.

In May this year, a delegation from the Ministry of Water Resources of China and the Department of Water Resources of Xizang Autonomous Region visited Nepal and made substantial progress with the Ministry of Energy, Water Resources and Irrigation and the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority of Nepal in promoting the establishment of a transboundary disaster information-sharing mechanism, the embassy said.

In August, a team from the Institute of Mountain Hazards and Environment of the Chinese Academy of Sciences visited Nepal for scientific research exchanges and shared China’s practical experience in glacial lake monitoring, said the embassy. On August 26, the day the flood disaster struck, the China Meteorological Administration held an urgent virtual meeting with the Department of Hydrology and Meteorology of Nepal to assess the disaster situation and share data simultaneously. /dl

articles.title: Flood damage to Nepal’s hydropower sector could run into billions
articles.summary: KATHMANDU — Nepal’s electricity authority says the devastating Bhotekoshi floods may have caused losses running into hundreds of billions of rupees across more than a dozen hydropower projects…

blocks.text: KATHMANDU — Nepal’s electricity authority says the devastating Bhotekoshi floods may have caused losses running into hundreds of billions of rupees across more than a dozen hydropower projects and electricity transmission infrastructure, far exceeding initial estimates by private sector developers.
The scale of the destruction has also raised urgent questions over how damaged projects will be rebuilt and who will bear the cost.
Rajan Dhakal, spokesperson for the Nepal Electricity Authority (NEA), said on Friday that the authority’s preliminary assessment pointed to losses worth hundreds of billions of rupees.

“For now, our priority is rescue operations, the search for missing people and restoring electricity supply,” Dhakal said. “There has been unimaginable loss of life and property. The Rasuwagadhi Hydropower Project has been completely washed away, while the Chilime project has been buried. Our preliminary estimate is that the damage runs into hundreds of billions of rupees.”

His estimate is substantially higher than that of the Independent Power Producers’ Association, Nepal (IPPAN), whose senior officials have put average losses in the sector at around Rs25 billion to Rs30 billion.
Uttam Bhlon Lama, senior vice-president of IPPAN, said older hydropower projects with ground-level powerhouses suffered extensive or complete damage.

“Newer projects with underground powerhouses and desanders have suffered comparatively less damage,” Lama said. “Overall, we estimate losses at around 25 to 30 percent of the total project cost, although a complete assessment is still pending.”
At least 13 hydropower projects, both operational and under construction, have been damaged in Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts.

Affected operational projects include the 20MW Langtang Khola project, which was in the testing phase, the 5MW Mailung Khola, 14.8MW Mailung Khola, a 25MW solar project operated by the NEA and its subsidiaries, the 14MW Devighat, 24MW Trishuli, 60MW Upper Trishuli A, 22MW Chilime and the 111MW Rasuwagadhi Hydropower Project.

Projects under construction that have been affected include the 37MW Upper Trishuli 3B, jointly owned by the NEA and Nepal Telecom, the privately developed 120MW Rasuwagadhi Bhotekoshi, the 6.42MW Upper Mailung A, the 216MW Upper Trishuli 1 and the 15.6MW Middle Trishuli Ganga project.
Insurance could play a crucial role in determining how quickly the projects are rebuilt.
While private hydropower projects are generally insured, government-owned infrastructure may not have comprehensive insurance coverage, according to industry experts.
Raju Raman Paudel, former executive director of the Nepal Insurance Authority, said insured projects should be able to claim compensation after losses are assessed.
“Once the damage is evaluated, insurance companies will make the payments,” he said. “But there are concerns that not all NEA projects are insured. That could create difficulties.”
Despite growing climate risks, many government-owned structures in Nepal remain uninsured, he said.

Sushil Dev Subedi, executive director of the Nepal Insurance Authority, said a detailed assessment of physical damage had yet to begin because rescue and relief operations remained the immediate priority.
“Once restoration work begins, insurance companies will start assessing the risks and losses, after which claims can be processed,” he said.

Some of the affected projects have investments from Nepali banks and multinational companies, he added, but all are insured through Nepali insurance companies. Licensed surveyors will assess the damage on behalf of insurers.

“It is rare for hydropower projects to be uninsured,” Subedi said. “All projects under construction are generally insured, but we cannot yet say with certainty whether every operational project has coverage. Everyone is still focused on rescue operations.”
He said insurance companies had the capacity to settle legitimate claims.
Mohan Kumar Dangi, president of IPPAN, said all private-sector hydropower projects had insurance coverage and developers expected to use insurance payouts to finance reconstruction.
“Some structures have been buried, and others may have been washed away,” he said. “The assessment will take some time.”

Projects with limited damage could be rebuilt relatively quickly, while severely damaged projects would take longer to restore, he said. IPPAN would also coordinate with the government on reconstruction.
Dangi said the damage was unlikely to create an immediate electricity shortage in Nepal because domestic generation currently exceeds national demand.
Flood shock hits stock market
The disaster has also rattled Nepal’s stock market, with hydropower and non-life insurance companies among the hardest hit.

Of the 13 sectoral indices traded on Wednesday, the hydropower index fell 2.84 percent and the non-life insurance index dropped 3.90 percent, reflecting investor concerns over the scale of losses and potential insurance liabilities.
On Thursday, while the benchmark Nepse index slipped by just 1.04 points, the hydropower sub-index fell by 19.48 points and the non-life insurance index dropped by 201.81 points.
Many of the companies whose share prices fell most sharply were hydropower projects located in Rasuwa and Nuwakot, the districts worst affected by the flooding.

Non-life insurers are particularly exposed because they provide coverage for damaged hydropower infrastructure. Investors fear that large insurance payouts could affect the companies’ profitability, brokers said.

The non-life insurance index fell by 404.05 points on Wednesday and another 201.81 points on Thursday. The hydropower index dropped 104.33 points on Wednesday and 19.78 points the following day, while the life insurance index fell by 175.13 points and 28.10 points respectively.

By contrast, the manufacturing and processing index rose by 41.44 points on Wednesday and 178.18 points on Thursday, as investors anticipated increased demand for construction materials during the reconstruction phase.

On Wednesday, shares in Rasuwagadhi Hydropower fell 15 percent, followed by Mailung Khola Hydropower at 14.99 percent, Trishuli Jal Vidyut at 12.95 percent, Upper Mailung Khola at 11.56 percent, Sanjen Jalvidyut at 11.18 percent and Chilime Hydropower at 10.12 percent.
Meanwhile, shares in Sarbottam Paints Industries rose 15 percent, Upper Hewakhola gained 10.43 percent and Kalinchok Hydropower increased 3.21 percent.
Broker Narendra Sijapati said the contrasting movements were a predictable response to the disaster.

“It is natural for the shares of hydropower companies operating in devastated areas to fall,” he said. “Non-life insurers also face major payouts. But reconstruction will eventually begin, and that will increase investment and demand.”

On Thursday, Upper Hewakhola fell 9.45 percent, Trishuli Jalvidyut 9.23 percent, Emerging Nepal 8.38 percent, Rasuwagadhi Hydropower 8.38 percent, Upper Mailung Khola 8 percent, Mailung Khola Jalvidyut 7.75 percent and Chilime Hydropower 5.15 percent.

Construction-related companies moved in the opposite direction. Sarbottam Paints rose 15 percent, followed by Ghorahi Cement at 8.19 percent, Sonapur Minerals and Oil at 5.05 percent, Bhagawati Hydropower at 4.72 percent, Palpa Cement at 4.53 percent and Shivam Cement at 4.17 percent.
Sijapati said the decline in hydropower shares would not necessarily extend across the entire sector, as companies outside the disaster zone remained largely unaffected.
He added, however, that broader investor confidence remained fragile, partly because of government policies and uncertainty surrounding the economic impact of the disaster.
He recalled similar market behaviour after Nepal’s devastating earthquake, when shares of cement companies rose on expectations of increased reconstruction activity.

The life insurance sector could also face pressure because travel insurance is mandatory for pilgrims undertaking the Kailash Mansarovar pilgrimage and the disaster has resulted in significant loss of life, he said. /dl

articles.title: Nepal issues fresh flood warning as 3,000 still missing
articles.summary: Rescuers are trying to reach dozens of hydropower workers trapped in flooded tunnels, but have been hampered by further rainfall.

image.caption: Several countries and the European Union have pledged millions in aidImage: Lhasa fire/Xinhua/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The combined death toll from the devastating floods in Nepal and Tibet rose to 750 on Sunday, with more than 3,000 people still missing, authorities said.
A fresh flood alert was issued after river levels rose again, while Tibetan authorities warned of a new barrier lake forming behind landslide debris.
Several scientists believe a glacier collapse in the Himalayas may have triggered Wednesday's disaster, sending huge volumes of water down a river valley.
Nepal flood survivors still searching for some 3,000 missing
What's the latest on the floods?
Nepal's disaster authority put the number killed on its side of the border at 734, while Chinese state media confirmed 16 dead in Tibet, an autonomous region of China.
Chinese authorities said the dead included over a hundred Nepalis and people from more than a dozen countries.
The Nepalese disaster agency issued a warning for fresh floods on Sunday and told residents around the Bhotekoshi River to remain on high alert as water levels rose.
Flood warning notices were sent to residents' phones, advising them to move to higher ground.
On the Tibet side, Chinese state media said monitoring drones on Saturday night had picked up a new lake forming from a barrier created by a landslide near the Gyirong border port.
Rescue teams near the Gyirong border port were moved because of the risk of the barrier bursting.

blocks.caption: Nepal's disaster agency has issued a warning for fresh floodsImage: Rajesh Kumar Singh/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Hydropower workers still trapped in tunnels
Meanwhile, Nepalese rescuers are trying to reach more than 100 hydropower workers believed trapped and still alive in tunnels swamped by flood debris.
Rescue teams are focusing on several hydropower projects on the Trishuli River, where more than 900 workers went missing during the floods.
At one of the sites on Saturday night, army teams used drills to break into the upper part of a mud-swamped tunnel to pump oxygen and deliver a camera inside.

Nepal's prime minister's office said that teams faced "continuous rainfall and difficult conditions" but had worked nonstop overnight, "making tireless efforts to search for and rescue those who may be trapped."

blocks.caption: Several thousand people remain missing, four days after the floods hitImage: Niranjan Shrestha/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Rescue effort bolstered by neighbors
Specialized teams from India and China have joined the rescue effort, along with Nepal's mountain rescue squad, which helps climbers on the world's highest peaks, including Everest.
Nepalese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Lok Bahadur Chhetri said the country needed assistance in such areas as tunnel rescue, DNA testing and identifying the victims.

The US State Department wrote on X that it would provide $3.6 million (€3.1 million) in "life-saving humanitarian assistance" to Nepal, including up to three months of emergency food aid for up to 10,000 flood-affected households.
The ⁠Red Cross estimates that more than 90,000 people are likely to have been affected by the disaster.

articles.title: Learning from cooperatives: Key lessons for media viability
articles.summary: How do we build trust and support among our audiences and sustain it? How can we diversify revenue streams without compromising editorial independence? How can democratic decision-making be…

blocks.text: How do we build trust and support among our audiences and sustain it? How can we diversify revenue streams without compromising editorial independence? How can democratic decision-making be maintained as a media organization grows and needs to move faster?

At the 14th edition of Festival Gabo, the most important gathering of journalists in Latin America, DW Akademie created spaces for reflection and discussion on the viability of journalism today. Journalists, founders of independent and community media outlets and media practitioners from across the region, including Colombia, Brazil, Venezuela, Bolivia and Argentina, explored independent journalism approaches. Particular attention was given to media cooperatives.

blocks.caption: Participants exchange ideas during one of the workshop sessions. Image: Benedikt Borchers/DW Akademie

blocks.text: “What characterizes cooperative media is their boldness,” said Ernesto Lamas, researcher and community radio pioneer from Argentina. “They aren’t afraid of new technologies or AI, while always remaining aware of the risks. They create media with their own rules, defining their own topics and aesthetics and find deep satisfaction in that editorial freedom.”

Lamas also gave a preview on an upcoming DW Akademie study, scheduled for publication at the end of 2026. Lamas conducted a series of interviews with representatives of media organizations organized according to cooperative principles — media organizations that operate on a non-profit basis and are oriented toward the public good. They seek to guarantee decent working conditions and employee participation in decision-making, while dedicating significant efforts to building active connections with their communities.
From TV to loans to funerals

William Galindo is director of Viboral TV, a local television channel located in a rural community in Colombia. The channel is part of a cooperative that offers various services to its members, including affordable credit, funeral services and internet access.

blocks.caption: From left to right, Ernesto Lamas, University of Buenos Aires, Gemma Terés Arilla, taz Panter Foundation, William Alberto Galindo Muñoz, Cooperativa Viboral Telecomunicaciones, Luis Rómboli, Cooperativa La Diaria, and Michelle Nogales Cardozo, Muy Waso, reflect on how to build sustainable media.…

blocks.text: According to Gallindo, being a cooperative means operating under strict state oversight and therefore requires highly organized administrative and financial management. The reward for these efforts is strong institutional recognition, which can translate into support from other entities, including financing.

The cooperative provides stability for the television channel and, according to Gallindo, the community media outlet is also a major asset for the cooperative because it reflects community life: local festivals, football matches and also local politics. Journalists are not afraid to criticize politicians because they do not depend on government funding. Instead, the channel is sustained through member subscriptions.
For , community is at the center of their work.
“92% of our revenue comes from subscriptions. We have a very close relationship with our community, with constant two-way communication,” Rómboli explained.

blocks.caption: Luis Rómboli, president of the La Diaria cooperative in Uruguay. Image: Benedikt Borchers/DW Akademie

blocks.text: Every day, the La Diaria newspaper sends a newsletter to 250,000 people. The newspaper transitioned to a cooperative in 2006 and during this process, received support from the German taz Panter Foundation. The foundation is part of the German newspaper taz – die tageszeitung, a longstanding example of cooperative journalism that emerged from the left-wing social movements of the 1970s in Germany.
“You don’t just have readers — you have a committed community,” said Gemma Terés Arilla, director of the taz Panter Foundation.

Agencia Mosquetero brought that relationship to a co-creational level. It is a communications and content agency affiliated with the alternative Colombian media collective El Cuarto Mosquetero, founded as a sustainable model to provide journalistic and creative services to organizations, unions and companies.

“Our greatest achievement is co-creating content with communities,” said Alejandra Mayorga, editor at El Cuarto Mosquetero. “Media viability requires diversifying revenue streams according to each media outlet’s reality, with editorial independence and transparency as fundamental principles.”
Tremendous challenges in a volatile environment

In some countries, bureaucratic barriers make it more difficult to establish a cooperative. Bolivia is one such example and one of the reasons why Muy Waso, a feminist community media platform, chose to establish a foundation instead. Nevertheless, their model is based on collective decision-making, as co-founder Michelle Nogales Cardozo stressed.

blocks.caption: Michelle Nogales Cardozo, Co-founder of Bolivia’s Muy Waso Image: Benedikt Borchers/DW Akademie

blocks.text: In a world of increasingly rapid change, media organizations must redefine their strategies in order to survive and fulfill their role in society. Cooperative models offer an alternative for those seeking to build media organizations with a social purpose.
1. Sustainability is about more than money
Participants viewed sustainability as not only an economic challenge, but also a social and political one.
2. Communities can be a crucial source of support
Strengthening relationships with audiences helps build trust and long-term support.
3. Revenue diversification and independence can go hand in hand
Cooperative models aim to balance financial viability with editorial autonomy.
4. There is no single cooperative model
Some media organizations embrace cooperative principles without necessarily adopting a cooperative legal structure.
5. Legal contexts matter
National regulations can either facilitate or complicate the creation of cooperatives.
6. Democratic governance requires effort
Maintaining participatory decision-making becomes more challenging as organizations grow.
7. Cooperatives can provide stability
The experience of Viboral TV shows how cooperative backing can strengthen the sustainability of community media.
8. Community support reinforces editorial independence
Membership and subscriber-based models can reduce reliance on other funding sources.
9. Audience engagement is a strategic asset
Experiences such as La Diaria demonstrate that involving communities can be a key factor in success.
10. Cooperative journalism deserves attention
Although it is not the only solution for the media sector, it offers valuable lessons for organizations committed to serving the public good. /dl

articles.title: Nepali Army rescues 2,697 people from flood-hit Rasuwa
articles.summary: KATHMANDU — The Nepali Army has rescued 2,697 people affected by flooding in Rasuwa district as of 7am on Sunday, using helicopters and ground teams. A total of 2,497 people, including 216…

blocks.text: KATHMANDU — The Nepali Army has rescued 2,697 people affected by flooding in Rasuwa district as of 7am on Sunday, using helicopters and ground teams.

A total of 2,497 people, including 216 foreign nationals, were evacuated by air from Timure, Syabrubesi, Dhunche and Mailung. The foreign nationals rescued include 121 Indians, 72 Chinese, 15 South Koreans, four Germans, two Americans, two Italians and one Omani. Ground teams rescued another 200 people, said the Nepali Army.
More than 8,300 Nepali Army personnel have been deployed across affected districts and are working in coordination with other agencies.

Meanwhile, efforts to locate the entrance to the 3A tunnel of the Trishuli Hydropower Project were temporarily halted after heavy rainfall from around 2am caused water levels to rise and flooded excavation areas. /dl

articles.title: Humanitarian crisis worsening in refuge for civilians fleeing Sudan’s civil war
articles.summary:
Conditions are deteriorating in city of El Obeid and camps on its outskirts, with more people arriving every day

Humanitarian conditions in the Sudanese city of El Obeid and two camps on its…

blocks.text: Humanitarian conditions in the Sudanese city of El Obeid and two camps on its outskirts are dire and deteriorating, according to people on the ground, as civilians displaced by fighting between the Sudanese Armed Forces and Rapid Support Forces (RSF) militia continue to pour in from the surrounding countryside.

The UN says more than 15,000 families have arrived since mid-July, joining more than 200,000 people who arrived in the first half of the year, according to government figures cited by Save the Children.

“The situation is very harsh and is deteriorating as El Obeid is receiving IDPs [internally displaced people] on a daily basis … The city is shockingly overcrowded,” said Maryam, a humanitarian volunteer whose name has been changed for her safety.
The new arrivals came on foot, carrying almost nothing, she said. “They also suffer from a shortage of food and they definitely arrive traumatised.”
The city, the capital of North Kordofan province, was home to around half a million people before the war broke out more than three years ago.

blocks.caption: Tens of thousands of people are living in tented camps around El Obeid.  Photograph: AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: While many of the new arrivals have been absorbed into the city, tens of thousands are living in two main tented camps. According to analysis of satellite data by the Yale Humanitarian Research Lab, 800 new tents appeared in one of the camps between 4 and 25 August.

“During my visit, I saw 450 arrivals coming from the surrounding villages just that morning,” said Paul Byars, the Sudan country director for the Danish Refugee Council, who was in El Obeid last week. “The authorities’ estimates are correct, that 85% of them are women and children. Most of the men are staying behind because this is the only time for farming.”
Civil war erupted in Sudan’s capital, Khartoum, about 250 miles (400km) north-east of El Obeid, on 15 April 2023, when a power struggle between the armed forces and RSF descended into open conflict.
Since then, about 11.3 million people have been displaced, more than a fifth of the population. Some parts of the country, including El Obeid and surrounding areas, are at risk of famine.

Estimates of the number of people killed in the war range from tens to hundreds of thousands. More than 10,000 people are thought to have been massacred by the RSF in El Fasher over two days when they seized the city in Sudan’s western Darfur region in October 2025 after an 18-month siege.

blocks.caption: The damaged interior of a lawyers' syndicate in El Obeid, reportedly targeted by the RSF in July. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: A surge in RSF drone strikes on El Obeid and nearby areas in June led the UN to warn that the city could face a repeat of what happened in El Fasher.

The number of strikes has since fallen. The armed forces also recaptured a key road leading north to Khartoum in late July, which at least partly lifted the threat of besiegement. However, drones are still killing and injuring civilians, while violence rages in the surrounding districts, pushing people to the city.

Recently, volunteers in El Obeid had noticed more “double-tap” drone strikes, where a second drone follows the first, hitting rescuers at the scene, Maryam said. “It is hard, so hard, living with this, hearing the sound of a drone hitting somewhere,” she said. “It’s very disturbing.”

Sudan’s civil war has become dominated by drones, accounting for half of all violent incidents, up from 4% at the start of the war, said Nohad Eltayeb, who monitors Sudan for Acled, a conflict tracking group.
Both sides used drones, but the RSF’s usage had become more volatile since the US war with Iran began to interrupt supply lines in February, she said. “They rely on fewer, very targeted strikes.”

So far this year, there have been 322 incidents of violence affecting civilians in the wider Kordofan region, compared with 388 for the whole of 2025, according to Acled data. While the RSF was responsible for half of those, the SAF has also killed and injured civilians. On 10 August, armed forces and an allied militia killed five civilians and injured 10 about 60 miles north-east of El Obeid, according to Emergency Lawyers, a non-governmental group.

With the threats to delivery trucks, food prices have rocketed. In north Kordofan in July, according to World Food Programme data, a litre of groundnut oil cost 17,000 Sudanese pounds (£21), up from 13,000 in June and 7,700 a year ago. The prices of wheat flour and goat and sheep meat have also more than doubled in the last year.

blocks.caption: Conditions in the camps around El Obeid are said to be poor.  Photograph: AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Meanwhile, El Obeid’s power and water infrastructure still has not fully recovered from RSF drone strikes in June.

“The main problem is the big [water] source that is in the north of the city has been severely damaged and it has not been repaired,” said Esperanza Santos, an emergency coordinator in Sudan for Médecins Sans Frontières. “The water pipes in the city have [also] been impacted. So mostly, both in the city – for example, in the hospital – and also in the IDP camps, they are relying on water trucking and it’s not enough.”

Conditions in the camps were poor too, Santos said. “In terms of sanitation, it’s very, very bad. It’s not enough. The ratio of latrines per person is impossible – there are more than 100 people for a latrine. So basically there is open defecation.”

Maryam said she and her fellow local volunteers remained committed, despite the difficulties. “The situation is deteriorating, but we are trying to stay together, to stay strong in the face of the drone attacks and the influx of IDPs … We are living with this and we hope things will become better.”

articles.title: Africa’s aging autocrats fight to stay in power
articles.summary: Power can be seductive, and many who possess it want to hold on for as long as possible. The leaders of China and Russia, for example, cleared the way for additional terms years ago, and in the…

blocks.text: Power can be seductive, and many who possess it want to hold on for as long as possible. The leaders of China and Russia, for example, cleared the way for additional terms years ago, and in the United States, the president occasionally speaks of another run for office, even though the US Constitution does not allow it.
From the perspective of Paul Biya, however, Chinese President Xi Jinping, Russian President Vladimir Putin and US President Donald Trump are still relatively new to office.
Cameroon’s president has been head of state since 1982. In 2025, Biya began his eighth term — which is officially due to end on November 6, 2032, just a few months before his 100th birthday.
The 93-year-old has given no official indication that he intends to step down, and the position of vice president remains vacant.
Paul Biya in Cameroon: A loyal leadership circle with one weak spot
During his 44 years in office, Biya has built a stable network of loyal allies that keeps the machinery of government running despite his lengthy absences.

The 93-year-old has now spent two and a half months in Geneva, Switzerland, continuing to issue decrees and make personnel decisions from abroad. In mid-June, his spokesperson denied rumors Biya was receiving treatment in a hospital and stated that the president was in good health.
“There is continuity, but that also means there is little momentum for reform within the government,” Beverly Ochieng, senior analyst at consultancy Global Risk, told DW.

And while Biya’s power apparatus has helped cushion the impact of the president’s long absence, that does not necessarily mean the most influential figures on the ground are united. After all, a post-Biya era is now in sight, and several of his allies are rumored to have ambitions of succeeding him.

“When everyone is lining up to potentially succeed Biya, it also means that the elites may begin challenging one another,” Ochieng said. Such rivalry, she warned, could lead to major disruptions, including the possibility of a military coup.
Analyst Levi Mboushou recently voiced similar concerns on DW’s AfricaLink podcast.

“Everyone feels the fear and uncertainty, but no one dares to look directly at it because we all have to deal with this repressive regime. You see something, but you say nothing. That is the situation in Cameroon at the moment,” he said.
Yoweri Museveni in Uganda: Signs of a dynasty?
Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni is only slightly younger, both in age and years in office.

The 81-year-old has been president since 1986 and, like Biya, recently embarked on another term. His succession also remains unresolved, although his son, Muhoozi Kainerugaba, has recently attracted considerable attention as head of the military.
According to Ochieng, the dynamics in Uganda are complex, not least because military elites and the ruling National Resistance Movement (NRM) have their own internal power structures.

blocks.caption: Is Muhoozi Kainerugaba (center, seen here in 2019) being groomed to eventually succeed his father? Image: Joseph Kiggundu/Photoshot/picture alliance

blocks.text: “Muhoozi has become the most visible figure primarily because he has a strong personality and enjoys the discreet backing of his father. His rise is not the result of support from either the NRM or the military leadership,” she said.
Kainerugaba is increasingly emerging as a political figure, including on issues beyond military affairs.

In early July, he ordered the closure of several media outlets. At the time, a source from an international foundation who requested anonymity told DW: “We are witnessing a transfer of power to the president’s son.”
A similar development has been unfolding for years in Equatorial Guinea, where Teodoro Obiang Nguema Mbasogo, who has ruled since 1979, appears to be gradually transferring power to his son.
Known by the nickname “Teodorin,” he has served as first vice president since 2016 and now also controls the military.

In June, Teodorin announced the resignation of the entire government on behalf of his father. Observers interpreted the move as a sign that he is gradually becoming the public face of state authority.
Whether Museveni will actually arrange his succession during his lifetime remains uncertain.
Ochieng believes that, in the event of a sudden power vacuum, Uganda could either hold constitutionally mandated elections or follow a scenario similar to that seen in Chad in 2021.
Then-President Idriss Deby was killed in clashes with rebels. The constitution was suspended, allowing his son, Mahamat Idriss Deby Itno, to take power.
Emmerson Mnangagwa in Zimbabwe: Party before people
Zimbabwe also amended its constitution this year, making it far less likely that President Emmerson Mnangagwa could be voted out of office.

In June, both chambers of parliament approved changes extending the terms of parliament and the president from five to seven years. Even more fundamentally, the president will no longer be elected directly by the people but by parliament, where the ruling ZANU-PF party enjoys comfortable majorities.

In July, the 83-year-old Mnangagwa signed the amended constitution into law. However, the opposition and some constitutional experts argue that a referendum should still be held. The government, by contrast, considers the constitutional amendment process complete.
“We are not surprised,” Chiedza Mlingwa, deputy spokesperson for the Constitution Defenders Forum, said at the time on DW’s AfricaLink podcast.

“The only thing one could be surprised by is the audacity, nothing else. We have observed this pattern since independence in 1980: ZANU-PF works to stay in power. The party does not believe in relinquishing power.”
Ochieng noted that countries such as Togo and Cote d’Ivoire have also implemented constitutional changes aimed at preserving power in recent years.

Meanwhile, in Senegal, a constitutional amendment is being discussed amid tensions between former allies at the top of the state, President Bassirou Diomaye Faye and Speaker of Parliament Ousmane Sonko, both of whom are significantly younger than the continent’s other long-ruling leaders.

“Even when legal safeguards exist, if they are not designed in a way that guarantees citizen participation, public debate, civil society engagement, or oversight by other institutions, then it becomes possible for unilateral decisions to be made at the highest levels of government,” said Ochieng.
The weakening of institutions to allow individuals to remain in power, she added, is not an African problem but a global one. /dl

articles.title: Pacific leaders to meet in Palau amid China, Taiwan tension
articles.summary: KOROR — Pacific island leaders will tackle transnational drug crime as they meet in Palau from Monday for a summit where tensions between Taiwan and China risk overshadowing regional priorities…

blocks.text: KOROR — Pacific island leaders will tackle transnational drug crime as they meet in Palau from Monday for a summit where tensions between Taiwan and China risk overshadowing regional priorities like climate change.
Palau, this year’s host of the 18-member Pacific Islands Forum, is among three members holding diplomatic ties with Taiwan and not China, a large creditor to many island states.
China, Taiwan and the United States are among the aid partners invited to the forum, although not the leaders’ meeting. Beijing has protested Taiwan’s invitation.
On Sunday, Taiwan’s foreign minister Lin Chia-lung cut the ribbon with Palau President Surangel Whipps at a ceremony handing over a fleet of electric buses donated by Taipei.
China retaliated against Lin’s arrival in Palau by declaring the tourism-dependent island an “unsafe” place for travellers, Whipps later told reporters.
Chinese tourists are the largest group of visitors to Palau, data shows.
The US Embassy issued a statement accusing China of attempting to “weaponize tourism to coerce Palau”.
“The Pacific is our home, not a theatre for geopolitical competition,” Whipps said in an interview on Sunday.

Tensions between the Pacific’s partners should not detract from island priorities of action on renewable energy, drug crime, food security and climate change, which had real impact on lives, he urged.
Island populations are struggling with rising fuel and food costs caused by the Middle East war.
Transnational policing
Around 110 police drawn from various Pacific islands will provide security at the forum, the first large-scale demonstration of Pacific-wide cooperation on policing.
Australia, the biggest forum member and aid donor, has led efforts for the Pacific to provide its own security, arguing there is no need for China to have police in Kiribati and the Solomons.
Whipps said the Pacific leaders would seek to build on policing ties to tackle drug crime.
Fiji, a major transport hub for the Pacific, is experiencing the world’s fastest HIV outbreak, driven by what health authorities say is risky injecting of methamphetamine.

Police seizures of cocaine and methamphetamine in Fiji, the discovery of abandoned “narco subs” in the Solomon Islands and drug packages washing to shore in remote islands have reinforced fears of drug cartels forming a Pacific Ocean trafficking highway.
A regional maritime response to rising drug crime will be discussed by the leaders, with Australia and Fiji expected to be major contributors if it is approved, Australian officials told AFP.
Whipps gave the example of a Chinese drug gang that had operated in Palau before moving to Fiji.

“Clearly the same people are roaming around the whole Pacific and is evidence of why we need to collaborate and share information. They are destroying our youth and destabilising our nations,” he said.
Tensions over China

Australian National University Pacific expert Graeme Smith told AFP “climate change is at the top of the Pacific priority list, but the challenge of transnational crime is growing with the outbreak of HIV in Fiji”.

Fourteen island leaders are expected in Palau, after pro-Beijing Kiribati said its leader could not attend and the Solomon Islands prime minister Matthew Wale left unexpectedly on Sunday, returning home to deal with a political crisis — a no confidence motion lodged against his leadership.
Solomon Islands had been China’s closest partner in the Pacific until Wale was recently elected, vowing to review a secret security pact and repairing ties with the US and Australia.

US deputy secretary of state Christopher Landau and US Coast Guard Commandant Admiral Kevin Lunday will arrive in Palau on Monday to strengthen ties with Pacific countries before travelling to Solomon Islands and Kiribati.
The East-West Center’s Henry Puna, previously the forum’s secretary general, told AFP that climate change should be the most important issue for Pacific leaders.
But the impact of China’s ballistic missile test into the region last month was still being felt.
The forum has been unable to issue a joint statement of condemnation after Kiribati and Nauru held out and leaders will continue to discuss it in Palau, Whipps said. /dl

articles.title: Russian-American heads Trump’s planned Caucasus trade route
articles.summary: Until recently, few people in the South Caucasus had heard of Konstantin Sokolov. Now the 52-year-old Russian-American businessman is at the center of new investment fund backed by US President…

blocks.text: Until recently, few people in the South Caucasus had heard of Konstantin Sokolov. Now the 52-year-old Russian-American businessman is at the center of new investment fund backed by US President Donald Trump.

In mid-July, Sokolov — who emigrated from Russia to the US at age 21 and later founded the investment firm IJS Investments in Chicago — was appointed to head a new investment fund of the US State Department.

The TRIPP+ EnterpriseFund, registered in the US as the Trans-Caspian Enterprise Fund and launched with more than $200 million (about €172.5 million) in capital, is expected to invest in countries across the South Caucasus and Central Asia and help finance the large-scale TRIPP infrastructure project, also known as the “Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity.”

The “Trump Route” is a transit corridor that aims to connect Azerbaijan with its autonomous exclave of Nakhchivan through Armenian territory. The ambitious infrastructure project is part of a peace deal that Armenia and Azerbaijan signed in August 2025 with US mediation. In early June 2026, Washington and Yerevan signed a framework cooperation agreement for the project.
Experts have said construction of the “Trump Route” fits Washington’s strategy of creating a trade corridor between Europe and the region that bypasses existing routes through Russia and Iran.
Sokolov buys up Russian assets in Armenia
Long before he was appointed to head TRIPP+, Sokolov had already established a foothold in Armenia.

In 2024, he acquired Viva Armenia, the country’s largest telecommunications provider. Despite its subsequent partial nationalization, Sokolov continued to expand his holdings. Recently, his companies also bought up the Armenian subsidiary of Russian telecom giant Rostelecom.

blocks.caption: In August 2025, Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev (left) and Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan (right) signed a joint declaration ‘peace road map’ after talks with Trump Image: Azerbaijan Presidency/Anadolu/picture alliance

blocks.text: An even more significant deal, however, was carried out largely out of the public eye: the purchase of the Teghut copper-molybdenum mine. The mine, which holds an estimated 450 million metric tons of ore and has Armenia’s second-largest reserves, had been taken over by Russia’s state-owned VTB Bank after the company accumulated massive debts. VTB is now under Western sanctions. According to Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty’s Armenian service, the deal was carried out through a third-party company.
“Sokolov wanted to avoid a direct deal with the Russian bank,” said Mkrtich Karapetyan, a Radio Liberty journalist who has been investigating the flow of foreign capital into Armenia.
Sokolov: Trump supporter, MAGA backer
While Armenia’s government and its supporters have welcomed the influx of Western capital into the country’s infrastructure projects, the opposition has highlighted serious risks.

Mesrop Manukyan, a lawmaker from the opposition Armenia Alliance, is among Sokolov’s most vocal critics in parliament. He said it’s alarming that a US investor has been able to acquire major stakes in the finance, mining and telecommunications sectors in just a few years.

Manukyan’s faction, which advocates close ties between Armenia and Russia, opposes the TRIPP+ project. It views the “Trump Route” as a disguised “extraterritorial corridor” and the “greatest threat” to Armenia’s security.

Despite his extensive investments, Sokolov remains largely unknown to the Armenian public. There are no official photos of him, and he generally avoids interviews with the local press during business trips.

His most recent visit to the capital, Yerevan, was in early August, when he met with Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan and Foreign Minister Ararat Mirzoyan. He was accompanied by Aryeh Lightstone, senior adviser to US special envoy Steve Witkoff.

In Western media, however, Sokolov is known not only for his business ventures in the US and Switzerland but also for his political involvement. Sokolov is a major donor to the US Republican Party and a Trump supporter. According to The Associated Press, he donated about $11 million to Trump’s MAGA movement over the course of a year.
‘Compromise’ between Moscow and Washington?
Benyamin Poghosyan of the Armenian think tank APRI sees two main reasons for Sokolov’s appointment to head the fund.
The first is political. Appointing an American with Russian roots could be “a subtle gesture by Washington aimed at easing Moscow’s fierce criticism of the project,” he told DW.

The second, however, is pragmatic. “Perhaps Russia has nothing to do with it at all. Sokolov may simply have been chosen because he has a deep understanding of the business environment in the former Soviet Union — and because he knows Armenia and how its government works,” said Poghosyan.

blocks.caption: Armenia and Azerbaijan were locked in a conflict over the Nagorno-Karabakh region for decades Image: Tofik Babayev/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: At the same time, the sheer scale of the investment and the financier’s Russian roots are fueling speculation in Armenia. Social media users in the country are debating whether Sokolov, who was born in St. Petersburg, could be a secret “compromise figure” between Moscow and Washington. Supporters of the theory point to the ease with which US companies have acquired formerly Russian assets subject to Western sanctions.

Other observers have refuted the idea, noting that Sokolov has publicly and sharply criticized the Russian government and its war against Ukraine. The funds provided by the US State Department, running through 2036, are seen as flagging Washington’s long-term strategic intentions in the region. During his visit to Yerevan, Aryeh Lightstone told Armenian news outlet CivilNet that the more than $200 million in initial funding could be viewed as a starting point for future investments.

Aram Sargsyan, head of the Republican Party of Armenia and an ally of Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan, also rejects the idea that Sokolov is a “compromise figure” for Moscow. He emphasized the practical value of Sokolov’s background, seeing it as an opportunity rather than a cause for concern.
“Sokolov has significant business contacts, understands the Russian mentality perfectly, speaks the language and knows how to work with relevant Russian institutions,” he said. /dl

articles.title: Serbia keeps EU, Russia in play ahead of key election
articles.summary: Smoke from the wildfires still hangs over parts of Serbia, but as the flames slowly recede another debate is taking shape in their wake — one that has less to do with firefighting and more with…

blocks.text: Smoke from the wildfires still hangs over parts of Serbia, but as the flames slowly recede another debate is taking shape in their wake — one that has less to do with firefighting and more with politics.

In early August, wildfires swept across Serbia, burning through more than 3,500 hectares (8,600 acres) in the Deliblato Sands Special Nature Reserve. Firefighters, soldiers and helicopters battled the flames for days.

Then a Russian Ilyushin Il-76 firefighting aircraft arrived in the southern city of Nis. Serbia had turned to Moscow for help, making Russia the first foreign country it asked to provide a firefighting aircraft. Pro-government media greeted its arrival with celebratory coverage, dubbing the aircraft the “Russian beast.”

“Considering that there are no firefighting aircraft of this capacity available within the European Union, the arriving Russian aircraft will significantly strengthen our capacities to fight the fires,” said Luka Causic, head of the Serbian Interior Ministry’s Department for Emergency Situations.
A pragmatic choice between EU, Russia — or a political signal?
The episode, however, was already being viewed through a geopolitical lens, as Serbia had sought Russian assistance before activating the EU’s emergency mechanism.

When it did call on the EU, the response was swift. Brussels mobilized four helicopters from its strategic rescEU reserve, based in Czechia, Romania and Slovakia, along with ground firefighting teams from Germany and Romania.

blocks.caption: Emergency services, including German firefighters, were on hand to help Serbia battle wildfires Image: Feuerwehr Bonn/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: President Aleksandar Vucic rejected the idea that turning to Russia first was a foreign-policy decision or a sign of Serbia’s political alignment with Moscow.

“As far as equipment and resources are concerned, we are a European giant. The helicopters we received from Europe to fight the fires are less capable than ours and have a lower carrying capacity than our own,” Vucic said during a visit to the Deliblato Sands.
Zelenskyy in Belgrade
The wildfire episode came less than two weeks after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy made his first official visit to Serbia.

The two presidents reaffirmed their support for each other’s territorial integrity, which is particularly significant for Belgrade because Ukraine does not recognize the independence of Kosovo . Kosovo declared independence from Serbia in 2008, which Belgrade still does not recognize.
But Vucic is also trying to keep the other side on board, said Vuk Vuksanovic, a political scientist and foreign policy lecturer at King’s College London.

Vuksanovic argues that Vucic’s engagement with Zelenskyy must therefore be portrayed in Moscow not as a fundamental shift in Serbia’s relationship with Russia, but as a response to Western pressure and Serbia’s own interests.
“Vucic is now trying to make sure that neither the West nor Russia becomes an open opponent during the election campaign,” said Vuksanovic.

“Zelenskyy was primarily received so that the ruling coalition could present itself to Europeans as a great friend of Ukraine. In the same way, Vucic is trying to present himself to the Trump administration as a great friend of Israel, primarily to ensure that neither the European Union nor the United States becomes an opponent of the ruling party during the election campaign,” he added.
Vucic’s room to maneuver is shrinking
The problem is that the room to maintain these relationships may be shrinking.
The deeper the confrontation between Russia and the West becomes, the harder it is for Serbia to remain close to both without facing pressure to choose.

The European Union increasingly expects candidate countries to align their foreign and security policies with those of the bloc. Serbia’s refusal to impose sanctions on Russia remains one of the most visible obstacles to closer alignment.

But Moscow, too, has reasons not to take Belgrade’s loyalty for granted, Vuksanovic said. He argued that Russia does not fully trust Vucic, even as Moscow continues to support his narrative about “color revolutions” — a reference to anti-government protests, in this case the student-led protests in Serbia that gathered pace in early 2025. Vucic and Russia have both portrayed the protests as Western-backed attempts to destabilize the government.

For Vucic, however, the longer-term question of Serbia’s ties with Russia can wait. The more immediate question is whether he will survive the election, tentatively scheduled for October, and remain in a position to preserve that delicate balance himself. /dl

articles.title: WhatsApp chat used to send cash for crime and extremism
articles.summary: The WhatsApp money launderers arranged cash transfers in the UK and around the world with no paper trail.

blocks.text: A WhatsApp group chat was used to send hundreds of millions of euros in cash around the world, funding organised crime and extremism with no paper trail, an investigation by European broadcasters has found.
The 532-member group chat, called "Traders of Greater Europe", was used to arrange cash transfers across borders for their clients, including to British cities such as Birmingham and London.
In one case, payments from Brussels went to militants from the Islamic State group (IS) in Syria.

The European Broadcasting Union (EBU) investigative journalism network, which includes the BBC, also found wider evidence of similar cash transfer systems being used in people smuggling and drug trafficking.

The group chat, which contained more than 82,000 messages sent between late February and December 2022, was first uncovered by Belgian investigating magistrate Vincent Guerra. An investigating magistrate is a judge who examines evidence in complex cases before trial and makes a recommendation about whether they should proceed.

Guerra said the number of transactions was "staggering" and the network covered "the entire planet". The case began as an investigation into terror financing, but "it became just a drop in the ocean of transactions", he said.

Members of the group chat sent messages in Arabic to each other to set up cash payments using the ancient hawala transfer system. Hawala involves a network of trusted money brokers who can arrange for funds to be sent around the world without any electronic record or physical transport of bank notes.

The system involves an agreement between two brokers, known as hawaladars, in different locations. One of the hawaladars is paid a sum of cash and the other agrees to supply the same sum, minus commission, to the recipient. The hawaladars agree to settle up all their transactions between themselves at a later date.
Hawala transfers are frequently used for legitimate purposes, such as immigrant workers sending funds home to support their families in countries with limited access to banks.

But criminals can also take advantage of hawala transfers to avoid the Swift system used for most international money transfers, where banks typically flag large transactions outside the normal course of business and are required to report any suspicious activity.

The Great Traders of Europe group was reserved for transactions over €5,000 (£4,279) and payments were often much larger. There is no indication that all those participating in the group were involved in handling criminal funds.
Hawala is illegal in many countries, including most of the EU, but is legal in the UK as long as the brokers are registered with Revenue and Customs (HMRC).

The cache of WhatsApp messages was obtained by the EBU following a 2024 court case in Belgium which convicted six money launderers, including Abu Adam, the head of the network in Brussels, and his number two, Abu Ahmed.

Belgian police had discovered evidence that the defendants had been sending money to IS, which was intended to help the wives of militants escape from detention camps in Syria. When they arrested Abu Adam, they discovered the Traders of Greater Europe group chat on his phone.

Guerra said it was like "hitting the jackpot", uncovering the inner workings of a vast, underground system. The phone also contained 6,000 photos of €5 notes showing the serial numbers and 6,000 photos of identity cards. These details are often used as unique identifying codes in hawala transactions, and the total number of notes and ID cards suggest Abu Adam had processed at least 12,000 transactions, Guerra said.
"This isn't just amateur work; it's professional, and at a level we could never have imagined," he said. "They're bankers with no government oversight."

The EBU also found further gangs across Europe using the hawala system for criminal activity. One former money launderer previously involved in European hawala networks, whom we are calling Frank, told the EBU he had been involved in transactions totalling several hundred million euros.

His first introduction to the hawala system had been at an office in a small town outside Rotterdam, he said. There, five or six messengers had arrived with money in about an hour and a half, transferring at least a million euros, he estimated.

"What I found out later is that it's not just about money. It's about the financing of terror. It's about drug trafficking. It's about prostitution and all sorts of other crap, to put it nicely," he said.
Cases in Austria have also revealed how the hawala system is bound up with people smuggling and violence.

In one case investigated by Austrian broadcaster ORF, part of the EBU network, Austrian police raided what they called "the biggest hawala office in Vienna". It was run from a kebab restaurant on a busy thoroughfare and which authorities say was used to make payments for people smuggling.

Two Syrian brothers who ran the operation were charged with human trafficking, as well as torturing and raping a courier who had lost €350,000 (£300,000), saying he had been robbed. They were convicted last year and sentenced to 18 and 8 years in prison respectively.
Austrian police and Europol also recently dismantled another people-smuggling ring financed through hawala, which officials said had transported about 100,000 people into Europe over 18 months.

Gerald Tatzgern, who leads human-trafficking investigations at Austria's Criminal Intelligence Service, the BK, told ORF that torture was a reality of people smuggling and was also used to maximise profits.

He said: "Videos of the torture are then sent to the families, saying that if they don't send another €1,000 or several thousand euros, then the person concerned - your son, your brother, your father - will suffer."

articles.title: India’s citizen-led school audits test limits of activism
articles.summary: The Indian activist movement dubbing itself the “Cockroach Janta Party (CJP)” shot to national prominence in May by leading weeks-long protests over a scandal involving highly competitive…

blocks.text: The Indian activist movement dubbing itself the “Cockroach Janta Party (CJP)” shot to national prominence in May by leading weeks-long protests over a scandal involving highly competitive entrance exams.
The student-led campaign put the government under intense political pressure and ended with the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan in July.
Now, the CJP is taking aim at India’s government schools, organizing volunteer visits to classrooms, documenting conditions and demanding accountability for problems.

Launched on August 15, Independence Day in India, the campaign asks parents, students and volunteers to inspect schools and record basic facilities including toilets, drinking water, electricity, classroom furniture and school buildings. The CJP has said the findings will be used to pressure authorities to make improvements.
The initial target is to audit 100 rural government schools over two months. It has also proposed giving recognition to village leaders who improve their schools.

Unlike the first campaign, which was based on street protests, the school audits require a more sustained form of local activism. Volunteers are expected to work consistently at the local level, document conditions and follow up with officials, parents and communities.

blocks.caption: Students celebrated in New Delhi after the resignation of India’s education minister in July Image: Raj K Raj/Hindustan Times/Sipa USA/picture alliance

blocks.text: The organization is dealing with different layers of the Indian administration. Responsibility for government schools is divided between state governments, local administrations and elected village bodies. The CJP is therefore set to tackle different rules and political interests across the country.
India has over a million government schools, according to Education Ministry data. They make up nearly 70% of all schools in the country but serve less than half of its 247 million schoolchildren.
CJP: ‘We are not afraid’
That scale has given CJP a vast field for its campaign. But it has also brought a new set of challenges.
The authorities are raising questions regarding rules and locations for the CJP scrutiny, as well as safeguards when children are present.
The response is already varying from state to state. Some authorities have ordered their own inspections, while others have restricted access or taken police action against CJP volunteers.
Authorities in Maharashtra and Rajasthan states have objected to school visits carried out without permission.
In one case, a complaint by school authorities resulted in police action against CJP members after they entered the premises to conduct an audit.
