In Rajasthan, restrictions have been imposed on outsiders entering government schools, as well as on filming, interviews and other forms of documentation. CJP volunteers in Rajasthan have also said they were attacked while inspecting a school.
“We are not afraid. We are seeking accountability from the government,” said CJP spokesperson Ashutosh Ranka.
Officials say schools are not open spaces

In the state of Uttar Pradesh, Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath has ordered officials to conduct on-the-spot checks of school facilities and directed police to register cases over what he called misleading videos about schools and colleges.
The CJP has said such measures undermine public scrutiny. Authorities have said schools are not open spaces for unauthorized inspections, particularly when children are present.
Vinita Gursahani Singh, managing trustee of We, The People campaign, which works on citizen empowerment, said the limits are set by law.

“Under the Right to Information Act, any citizen can inspect schools but you need to submit an application. And that makes sense as there has to be consideration for students and teaching,” Singh told DW.
“All public scrutiny is legitimate. It is our job to scrutinize. But the scrutiny has to follow process. It has to be even-handed. What applies to one citizen must apply to all,” she said.
Can activists serve as inspectors?
The CJP maintains government schools are publicly funded institutions and citizens have a legitimate right to ask how they are functioning.
Its volunteers use standardized audit forms to record conditions and send their findings to the CJP, which has said it will use the material to press local administrations to respond.

But critics question whether citizen activists can assume the role of inspectors. There are concerns about whether volunteers have the expertise to assess safety or infrastructure problems and how allegations posted on social media are verified.
Mohandas Pai, an education advocate, supports CJP’s focus on government schools but disagrees with its methods.
“I like young people taking interest in school education. It’s a broken system, and we need reforms,” Pai told DW.
But he objected to large groups entering schools and questioning headmasters and children.
“You can’t just barge into a school just because you think you are entitled to do it,” Pai said, stressing that “children have to have a safe, secure environment.”
Pai said the CJP should instead send small teams with permission, collect systematic data, publish regular reports and use the evidence to pressure governments.
CJP spokesperson Saurav Das rejected the argument that the campaign should rely on conventional channels, saying such approaches have failed to bring meaningful change.
Responding to Pai on X, he challenged him to join the next school visit and show the volunteers how it should be done.
Questions of student privacy
The audit campaign has also raised questions about privacy, consent and disruption of teaching when volunteers enter schools, film inside classrooms or question students.
However, Kavita Srivastava, president of the People’s Union for Civil Liberties (PUCL) Rajasthan, opposes restrictions on outsiders entering schools and taking photos and videos in her state.

“Activists were visiting government schools to document their condition and demand accountability. Protecting children’s privacy should not be used to prevent legitimate public scrutiny of government schools,” Srivastava told DW.
A new role for the CJP
Activist Amrita Johri said the CJP’s first campaign tapped into a longstanding accountability gap in India’s examination system, which cost millions of young people time and money.
“The demand for accountability had popular resonance because there was no real response from the government,” Johri told DW.
She backed the school audit campaign, saying public scrutiny should be welcomed.

“Public audits are an integral part of citizens’ right to information and should be welcomed as an opportunity to fix accountability,” she said. Johri added that the CJP needs to train volunteers, document problems and follow up with authorities to make the campaign effective. /dl

articles.title: Highest heavy rain warning issued in central Japan’s Fukui
articles.summary: Japan’s weather agency issued Sunday a special heavy rain warning for some areas in Fukui Prefecture, central Japan, and around 244,000 people have been urged to take emergency safety measures…

blocks.text: Japan’s weather agency issued Sunday a special heavy rain warning for some areas in Fukui Prefecture, central Japan, and around 244,000 people have been urged to take emergency safety measures amid reports of mudslides and vehicles stranded on flooded roads.

The Level 5 warning, the highest for heavy rain, was issued for the cities of Fukui, Ono and Katsuyama, indicating that a disaster has likely occurred or is imminent. The Japan Meteorological Agency later lowered it to Level 4, but it still means residents should evacuate from affected areas.
Houses and roads were inundated and rivers swelled due to heavy rain. Around 111,000 people in five municipalities have been urged to evacuate.
The Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism may take the emergency step of discharging water from a dam in Sakai to secure more room as water levels are rising.
In the 24 hours to Sunday morning, Katsuyama, Sakai and Fukui received a record rainfall of over 300 millimeters.
“It’s dangerous if water levels continue to rise. I hope the rain will let up,” a man in his 30s said in Katsuyama.
Earlier, the weather agency had warned that it might issue a special heavy rain warning for more areas.
Heavy rain is forecast for western to eastern Japan on Sunday as atmospheric conditions are unstable.
The Hokuriku region, including Fukui, may receive up to 120 mm of rain while 80 mm is forecast for the Chugoku region in the 24 hours through 6 a.m. on Monday, according to the agency. /dl

articles.title: Vietnamese coffee farmers ride China’s durian wave
articles.summary: DAK LAK, Vietnam — Vietnam’s Central Highlands produces around one sixth of the world’s coffee, but farmers are switching their traditional crop for durian to cash in on surging…

blocks.text: DAK LAK, Vietnam — Vietnam’s Central Highlands produces around one sixth of the world’s coffee, but farmers are switching their traditional crop for durian to cash in on surging Chinese demand for the pungent “king of fruits”.
“You can live okay with coffee, but it’s durian that makes you rich,” said Pham Xuan Lan, as he showed AFP journalists around his farm.
Blessed with a tropical climate and rich basalt soil, the lush Central Highlands produces vast quantities of robusta beans, and Vietnam trails only Brazil in coffee output.
But the area dedicated to durian has soared more than fivefold to 200,000 hectares (494,000 acres) nationwide over the past decade, according to the agriculture ministry.
Vietnam only officially entered the Chinese durian market after a 2022 trade protocol but last year became the country’s biggest supplier by volume, ending Thailand’s near two-decade dominance.
Lan was an early adopter, diversifying his crop two decades ago and now boasting 400 durian trees in Ea Knuec commune, part of Dak Lak province.
They produce 60 tonnes of the sweet yet smelly fruit, which is driven in frozen containers thousands of kilometres north into China.
The 56-year-old expects to make $76,000 this year — against $10,000 had he stayed with just coffee.
“With durian, I bought a car, houses for my children and built a villa for my family,” he said, his affluence evident around him.
Other local farmers have followed suit, focusing on the premium Ri6, Musang King and Dona varieties.

During the August-October harvest, Dak Lak’s roads are packed with trucks loaded with the spiky fruit, and at a durian festival this month, 525 vehicles formed what the Guinness World Records declared the largest ever parade of fruit-carrying vehicles.
Billions of views
The boom is driven by demand from China, fuelled by a combination of expanding supply and growing popularity on social media, particularly among young people.
On Douyin, China’s equivalent of TikTok, videos of users cracking open fruit with their bare hands have been watched billions of times.
“This tastes really sweet. It’s almost like it’s been coated in sugar,” said Douyin influencer Liulianzi in a clip liked more than 17,000 times.
Once a luxury food, increased competition between Thailand and Vietnam and improved transport links have helped cut prices and make the fruit more affordable.
At a durian tasting event in Beijing last month, Ada Song told AFP that she had spent almost 1,000 yuan ($150) on the fruit in recent weeks.
“I have tried nearly 20 different varieties,” Song said.
Durian “tastes just as sweet as cake, without the greasiness and heaviness”.
China imported almost $7.5 billion worth of fresh durian last year, a near 12-fold rise from 2015.
Now Beijing is seeking to boost its homegrown produce, with more than 3,000 hectares of plantations on the southern island province of Hainan, which has a similar climate to northern Vietnam.
But “our Hainan durians will always be just a supplement to Southeast Asian durians”, acknowledged Feng Xuejie, a durian expert at the Hainan Academy of Agricultural Sciences.
“It’s not even a competition.”
Improving quality
Vietnam’s durian exports are expected to reach $4 billion this year, up from $180 million in 2021 — 90 percent of them going to its northern neighbour.
But in the Central Highlands there are concerns about the reliance on China, as well as the risks of oversupply as more farmers join the rush.
Many anxiously eyed a recent price crash in Malaysia, blamed on an unusually bumper harvest.
Many farmers there have also switched to durian, focusing on premium varieties and fresh fruit, although the country has only a small slice of the Chinese market.
Vietnam’s government warned in early August of the “risks of oversupply and loss of quality control as the planted area is increasing rapidly”.
Farmers warn durian is not a one-way bet, requiring a strict mix of humidity, water and fertilisers.
Lan likened growing it to “raising a child — I can give you all the tricks but I cannot guarantee you similar success”.
He still grows coffee as his land is leased from a coffee company, allowing him to hedge his bets.
For some, the durian dream has already turned sour.
Hung, a farmer who gave only one name, switched entirely from coffee to durian five years ago, but switched back two years ago, admitting it was too hard to produce the quality required.
“I could not do it. I failed,” the 42-year-old said. “So I would never go back to durian again.” /dl

articles.title: Iceland EU referendum on a knife edge as counting continues
articles.summary: A vote on whether to resume membership talks with the European Union is too close to call.

blocks.text: Iceland's closely fought referendum on whether to resume membership talks with the European Union is going down to wire, with the result too close to call.

Based on the first 153,197 votes counted of the 270,000 voters eligible, 50.1% rejected the government's proposal, while 49.9% said yes, public broadcaster RUV said, with just 435 votes splitting them.

Prime Minister Kristrún Frostadóttir's centre-left government promised to hold a referendum by 2027, but brought it forward because of international tensions, including US President Donald Trump's threats against Greenland.
However, debate in this island nation of almost 400,000 people centred more on its fishing industry rather than security concerns.
Already part of the EU's single market and Schengen border-free zone, EU membership would bring Iceland into the customs union and eventually the euro.
Iceland began its application to join the EU in 2009 in the wake of the 2008 financial crisis and the collapse of Iceland's banking system.
Its application was already well advanced when a eurosceptic government came to power in 2013 and put talks on hold. Fishing rights was the biggest obstacle then - as it remains today.

Fish and marine industries account for almost 40% of Iceland's exports and many No voters feared they would cede some control of their lucrative fishing grounds under the EU's common fisheries policy.
The referendum campaign has fuelled debate about Iceland's place in the world, Frostadottir said after casting her ballot in the capital on Saturday.
"This is a great day, we've been waiting for this for years to be able to have a vote," Frostadottir said, adding that her government would continue its work regardless of the outcome.
The question on the ballot was: "Should Iceland resume accession negotiations with the European Union?"
A Yes vote would not be a final decision on joining the EU, but a move towards an accession agreement, which would then have to be approved by a second referendum.
Equally, the No vote would not rule out the chance of Iceland resuming talks in the future.
While economic issues dominated the referendum campaigns, security concerns also featured.
Iceland is a founder member of Nato but it has no military and relies on its allies for defence.
The country has backed Ukraine during Russia's full-scale invasion and officials have been alarmed by Russia's increased maritime manoeuvres near the island.
Trump's expressed interest in taking over Greenland has also raised concerns.

articles.title: Nepal floods: A disabled couple offer strangers the little they have
articles.summary: KATHMANDU — On a hillside in Dabile of Bidur Municipality-10 stands a lone house with a corrugated zinc-sheet roof. There are no other houses nearby. From the house, the only view below is of a…

blocks.text: KATHMANDU — On a hillside in Dabile of Bidur Municipality-10 stands a lone house with a corrugated zinc-sheet roof. There are no other houses nearby. From the house, the only view below is of a settlement devastated by Wednesday’s flooding of the Bhotekoshi River. Concrete houses lie submerged, while those on the opposite bank stand intact but eerily deserted.
Yet since the flood, the small house has rarely been without guests.

On August 16, the day the flood struck, 31 students and teachers who escaped the disaster spent the night there. The house became a safe haven for those who fled the nearby Uttargaya Public Secondary School.

Since then, it has become a refuge for people arriving in search of relatives missing in the flood. Between 15 and 20 people come here every day. At the edge of a forest, the house has become a place where people exhausted from walking in the sun can find drinking water, a meal and a place to sleep. More than 200 people have taken shelter here since the flood.
With no other houses around, it has become a sanctuary for families searching for relatives swept away by the flood and landslides, as well as for those who fled to save their lives.

The homeowners, Prem Bahadur Tamang and his wife, Maiya, are both disabled. Prem Bahadur has a spinal injury and can barely move around the house with the help of a walking stick. Maiya has difficulty moving her left leg. Despite their own physical limitations, the couple continue to take in anyone who comes to their doorstep. They do not let their guests go hungry.

blocks.caption: With no other houses around, it has become a sanctuary for families searching for relatives swept away by the flood and landslides Angad Dhakal/TKP

blocks.text: Government support for food and shelter has yet to adequately reach the area. In its absence, the Tamang couple have been helping those in distress with whatever little they have.
Asked how they make a living, Maiya says her husband receives a monthly old-age allowance of Rs3,000 and she receives Rs2,000. Their children also send them money occasionally.
“That is how we survive,” she says.
The grain they grow on their hillside farmland does not last the year. The couple also complain that they cannot protect their crops from monkeys.
On the day of the flood, Prem Bahadur was sitting outside his house when the Bhotekoshi began roaring. He approached the river with the help of his walking stick and was alarmed by what he saw.
“Look, the flood is destroying everything,” he recalls telling Maiya as he called her to see the river.

“People were swept away and houses were buried right before our eyes. We were in no condition to go and rescue anyone. We kept watching the Bhotekoshi, thinking the flood would not reach this high. But within seconds, Betrawati Bazaar had turned into a riverbed. The road used by vehicles was swept away. The school was submerged and school buses were buried.”
Prem Bahadur, who has lived in the area for four generations, says he had never witnessed such a disaster.
“It did not even look like a flood. It looked as if a volcano had erupted,” he says.
The couple say they feel they must do whatever they can to help people affected by the disaster.
Maiya says their stock of rice and lentils is running low. Despite her physical limitations, she cooks for the people who come to their home. Some guests cook for themselves.

“What else can we do? When things are normal, everyone can cook and eat on their own. Who would come looking for our house? It is at times like this that we have to help. We do whatever we can,” she says.

Her brother-in-law, Juhanlal Tamang, is also taking shelter there with his family after losing their home. Five members of his family are staying at the house. Juhanlal’s grandson was swept away by the Bhotekoshi and remains missing.

Haribahadur Rai, whose family members are also missing, is sheltering there as well. His house at Angitar was swept away. His wife, granddaughter, mother-in-law and father-in-law are among those missing.
The couple have taken in several families in similar circumstances.

“Although the house is small, we are all living and sleeping inside and outside, sharing our joys and sorrows,” Maiya says. “We are not in a position to go out and bring food and water. If supplies could come from somewhere, at least we would not have to send away people who come here for shelter on an empty stomach.”
She says they have enough rice and lentils for only a few more days.

The couple have two sons and two daughters, but none lives with them. Their eldest son, Bishal, is in India for work. Their younger son, Buddha, used to drive an auto-rickshaw along the Trishuli-Betrawati route, earning a living for himself while also helping his parents.
The Bhotekoshi flood not only swept away Buddha’s auto-rickshaw but also destroyed the route on which he worked.
“What are we going to do now?” Buddha asks, his face downcast. “My parents are disabled and our family is struggling. I would do any labouring job if I could find one.”
No government agency has yet been able to reach the area. Bodies floating in the river have begun to decompose, while the bodies of people trapped inside houses have yet to be recovered.
Amid the devastation, the Tamang couple’s house is the only one still standing intact. /dl

articles.title: Nepal: Rescuers battle treacherous terrain, shortages to find missing
articles.summary: KATHMANDU — On Friday afternoon, an Armed Police Force rescue team reached the wreckage of a security post in Timure, a remote settlement in Rasuwa bordering China. The rescuers were searching…

blocks.text: KATHMANDU — On Friday afternoon, an Armed Police Force rescue team reached the wreckage of a security post in Timure, a remote settlement in Rasuwa bordering China.
The rescuers were searching through the debris left by Wednesday’s devastating flood when one of them heard something unexpected: a child crying.

“At the surface, nothing was visible,” said APF Deputy Inspector General Netra Bahadur Karki. “We suspected someone was trapped beneath the debris. The team immediately began digging through the collapsed structure and successfully pulled a six-year-old girl out alive.”

The team belonged to the APF’s Collapsed Structure Search and Rescue unit, created in 2011 for major disasters. It has 285 trained personnel equipped to cut through concrete, steel and timber in difficult terrain. Members are also trained in combat medical care.
The girl was stabilised at the scene and taken to the Border Outpost in Timure. Bad weather prevented her immediate evacuation to hospitals in Dhunche or Bidur.
Her rescue was one of many taking place across the flood zone as Nepal’s security forces race against time to find people still trapped, missing or cut off.

The APF has deployed 4,203 personnel in specialist teams, including search-and-rescue dog squads, diving teams, rope rescuers, medical units, drone operators and personnel managing temporary holding centres.
“Our dog squads are locating five to seven bodies daily based on scent cues,” Karki said.

The disaster struck at about 8:40 am on Wednesday, when a huge surge swept down the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli river corridors, destroying roads, bridges, settlements and other infrastructure across central Nepal.
Seven Nepali Army helicopters and eight private aircraft have since been flying rescue and relief missions.
Among those deployed are troops from the Army’s elite Ranger Battalion. On Friday, they rescued four workers trapped inside an intake tunnel at Rasuwa Hydropower Project.
The tunnel entrance had been buried under thick slurry and the surrounding terrain was so badly altered that rescuers could not immediately locate it.

“The entire land structure had shifted; there was no visual landmark left to identify the entrance,” said Brigadier General Rajaram Basnet, the Army spokesperson, who is coordinating military operations from the Bidur barracks.
Army officers worked with project engineers and used structural plans to determine the tunnel’s location. Military engineers then used specialised equipment to break through the obstruction.
Images from the rescue show workers crawling towards the light through thick mud as soldiers moved in to extract them.

Rescuers lowered a heavy basket from a hovering helicopter and, secured by harnesses, crawled through the mud to reach the trapped men. The four survivors were then lifted out and flown to Kathmandu for treatment.
The operation illustrates the central problem facing rescue teams: in many places, the flood has not simply blocked access but erased the landscape itself.

Across the river basin, 84 frontline officers from the Army, Nepal Police and APF are involved in high-risk searches. In total, 4,811 Nepal Police personnel have been deployed for rescue, body recovery and logistics.
By 3:30 pm on Saturday, security forces had recovered 669 bodies from eight districts downstream, according to Senior Superintendent Abi Narayan Kafle, the police spokesperson.
Police commanders have positioned retrieval teams along the river corridor from Rasuwa to the southern plains, using drones to scan riverbanks and debris fields.
When sensors detect human remains beneath wreckage or sediment, ground teams equipped with hydraulic cutters and other power tools move in.
Once a body is recovered, it is tagged, placed in an airtight body bag and taken to a designated hospital.
Authorities record photographs and distinguishing features and, when necessary, collect fingerprints and biological samples for identification.

The scale of the disaster is already overwhelming those systems. Police say nearly 2,000 people have been reported missing by relatives in Makwanpur, Dhading, Kavre, Sindhupalchok, Dolakha, Ramechhap, Sindhuli, Chitwan and Nuwakot, while figures for Rasuwa were still being compiled.

“Given the sheer volume of casualties, storing bodies indefinitely is impossible,” a senior police field commander said. Authorities are therefore preparing emergency procedures for DNA sampling, fingerprinting, detailed records and tagged burials.
Home Minister Sudan Gurung has said the immediate priority is to save lives.
“Our security personnel are working without sleep,” Gurung said. “Until a missing person’s body is found, our operational assumption is that they are still alive and awaiting rescue.”
Helicopters have become the main lifeline for communities cut off by destroyed roads and bridges.

blocks.caption: Nepali Army personnel rescue people trapped inside a hydropower project tunnel in Rasuwa following the Bhotekoshi flood. Photo: Courtesy of Nepali Army

blocks.text: At the Army Barracks in Battar, Bidur, and at the Dhunche helipad, aircraft are taking off and landing continuously. Outside the razor-wire perimeter in Bidur, families wait and watch every incoming helicopter.
On Friday, Gurung went to speak to them. The meeting quickly heated up as angry relatives questioned the government over warnings and the speed of the rescue response.
“If the administration had alerted us the moment the surge crossed the northern border, the entire bazaar could have been evacuated in time,” one resident shouted through the fence.
Gurung defended the crews operating in narrow mountain valleys in dangerous weather. He cited the tunnel rescue as evidence that teams were reaching trapped victims.
Among those waiting was Nani Chaulagain, whose relatives remain trapped near the Trishuli Hydropower complex while her injured husband is being treated in Kathmandu.
“I don’t even have the money to travel to Kathmandu to be with my husband,” she said. “My family members are still stuck up there, and nobody can tell us when the helicopters will reach them.”

Police estimates suggest that about 100 people remain stranded around Timure. Preliminary reports also put the number unaccounted for at around 200 near the Mailung Upper Trishuli-A site, another 200 in Syaphrubesi and Haku, at least 50 at Tiru Secondary School in Uttargaya Rural Municipality-1 and 10 at the Save the Children compound in Biruwadanda.
Yet police face a basic limitation: they have no aircraft of their own.

“We have highly trained disaster response personnel on the ground, but because the Nepal Police owns no aircraft, we cannot deploy our units independently,” a senior police officer said. “In many remote sectors, our officers can only move when paired with Nepali Army helicopter missions.”

A police inspector in Rasuwa said emergency calls to the hotline number at 100 continue to come from stranded villagers, but ground teams often cannot reach them because roads have been destroyed and air transport is limited.
The disaster has revived a long-running debate over whether Nepal Police should have its own aviation capability.

Former Inspector General of Police Achyut Krishna Kharel wrote in his 2018 autobiography about repeated difficulties securing helicopter support during the Maoist conflict in the 90s. Proposals for police helicopters were submitted in 1996 and 1997, and a purchase was approved by the government in 2000 before the decision was reversed.
Successive police chiefs, including Rabindra Pratap Shah, Kuber Singh Rana, Sarbendra Khanal and Dhiraj Pratap Singh, later renewed calls for dedicated aviation assets.
“The lack of dedicated air assets for the police remains a critical bottleneck,” Singh said.
The APF faces the same problem. A senior officer said the force had repeatedly sought light helicopters for disaster response, but the proposals had not been approved.
The need for specialised equipment is equally pressing.

Nepali Army’s former Colonel Ratindra Khatri, a disaster management specialist, said the first 72 hours after a disaster are the most critical for locating survivors, although people can survive much longer in exceptional circumstances.

“Statistically, the vast majority of life-saving extractions occur within the first 72 hours,” Khatri said. “That initial window closed on Saturday morning, meaning operations must maintain absolute, maximum intensity.”
As the window narrows, rescuers are also battling severe shortages of equipment.
Police teams in Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading and Chitwan initially held 765 body bags and had used 194 by Saturday. Another 77 were being requisitioned from unaffected districts.
Field teams have also reported shortages of chainsaws, power tools and heavy-duty cutting equipment needed to clear trees, structures and debris.
Nepal has expanded the response by bringing in Nepal Red Cross volunteers and military recruits undergoing basic training for logistics and distribution work.

The government has also begun relying on specialised international assistance. After initially saying domestic forces had sufficient capacity, authorities later coordinated with India for a team of tunnel rescue specialists as the complexity of underground rescues became clearer.
Former Additional Inspector General of Police Thule Rai, who specialises in disaster logistics, said the scale of the destruction required sustained deployments across the entire river corridor.

“We need maximum boots on the ground,” Rai said. “Because the Trishuli river corridor is devastated, from the high border passes all the way to the southern plains, small deployments are ineffective.”
He said rescuers also needed advanced technical skills because unstable riverbanks and damaged structures posed serious risks to rescue teams themselves.

Anil Pokhrel, former chief executive of National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, said specialised equipment capable of detecting survivors beneath mud and collapsed structures could significantly improve operations.

“When I headed the authority, we attempted to procure these systems, but faced acute global supply shortages,” Pokhrel said. “Securing such equipment now will not only aid current operations but build long-term national resilience.”

By 8 pm on Saturday, the NDRRMA said 7,514 people had been rescued or otherwise assisted nationwide. The authority said 191 people had been pulled from flooded hydropower tunnels, 517 stranded people had been airlifted on Friday alone and 717 foreign tourists had been evacuated from high-altitude trekking routes.
For military commanders, however, the priority remains the same: find those who may still be alive.
“Ranger units are deployed across virtually every accessible sector in Rasuwa,” Basnet said. “Our primary focus remains on search and rescue for the living, rather than body recovery.” /dl

articles.title: Nepal to preserve DNA before burial of unidentified flood victims
articles.summary: KATHMANDU — Prime Minister Balendra Shah said on Saturday that the government would preserve DNA samples and other identifying evidence from bodies that cannot be identified before taking steps…

blocks.text: KATHMANDU — Prime Minister Balendra Shah said on Saturday that the government would preserve DNA samples and other identifying evidence from bodies that cannot be identified before taking steps to bury or otherwise manage them.

In a statement posted on social media on Saturday evening, Shah said only unidentified bodies would be handled by the government, while those identified by their families were being handed over to relatives.

“Only bodies that cannot be identified will be managed by the government after preserving DNA and other evidence that could help establish their identity,” he said. He urged the public not to be misled over the government’s handling of the dead.
Prime Minister Shah said that 675 bodies had been recovered so far from different locations in Rasuwa, Dhading, Nuwakot, Chitwan, Tanahun, Gorkha, Nawalparasi East and Nawalparasi West.
The recovered bodies are being placed in airtight bags and managed under the Unidentified and Unclaimed Bodies Management (First Amendment) Directive, 2026, he said.

The devastating flood that struck the Bhotekoshi river in Rasuwa on August 26 caused extensive loss of life and damage to property and infrastructure along the river corridor, including in Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading.
Shah said the government had intensified search, rescue, treatment, relief and communications restoration operations immediately after the disaster.
The response is being carried out in coordination with federal, provincial and local authorities, he said, with government agencies working at full capacity to protect those affected.
“Saving the lives of every affected citizen remains the government’s first priority,” Shah said.
He said the government would remain alongside affected communities and continue rescue and rehabilitation efforts until tangible results are achieved. /dl

articles.title: Floods wipe out Nepal local governments’ ability to lead rescue, relief
articles.summary: KATHMANDU — In the aftermath of catastrophic flooding in the Bhotekoshi river, disaster management efforts in the severely affected Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts have lurched into a deep crisis.…

blocks.text: KATHMANDU — In the aftermath of catastrophic flooding in the Bhotekoshi river, disaster management efforts in the severely affected Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts have lurched into a deep crisis.

Local governments—constitutionally mandated as the primary line of response during natural disasters—have themselves been overwhelmed and physically dismantled by the flooding, crippling rescue, relief, and data collection operations across the region.

In Gosaikunda Rural Municipality of Rasuwa, the vice-chair Pratima Tamang, two ward chairpersons and several employees are out of contact. According to chairman Kaisang Nurpu Tamang, seven members of his own family are also missing; the rural municipality office and two ward offices were washed away by the floods.

“My rural municipality has more than 2,000 people, including the vice-chair, two ward chiefs and seven members of my own family, who have gone missing in the flood,” Tamang told Kantipur. “The vice-chair has been out of contact since the flood and the search is continuing. How can we work in such a situation?”

Ward 5 chief Dawa Mingmar Tamang and ward 2 chair Kami Chhiring Tamang are among those missing, according to Gosaikunda’s executive member Pema Dorje Ghale. Ward 2 members Sonam Chhiring Ghale and Kami Shedar Ghale are also out of contact.
The vice-chair Pratima Tamang went out of contact from Syaphrubesi after the flood. The rural municipality’s ward 2 office in Timure and ward 5 office in Syaphrubesi were also swept away.

“Roads and electricity are gone, and telephone connections are difficult,” said chairman Tamang. “There is fear among residents, elected representatives and employees who are safe. Even so, we are trying as much as we can for rescue and relief.”

The August 26 flood has struck at the heart of the country’s disaster response system. Under the constitution, disaster management is both a local responsibility and a shared responsibility of the federal, provincial and local governments.

Local governments are also required by law to prepare disaster response plans, identify and map risk areas, coordinate search and rescue and relief, maintain disaster-related data and work with other levels of government and non-state actors.
But in the local units along the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers, the institutions responsible for those tasks have themselves become victims.

Krishna Bahadur BK, section officer in Gosaikunda Rural Municipality, said assistant accounts officer Kaisang Dindup Tamang, ward 2 secretary Prakash Acharya, employees Khambu Bohara, Kopila KC and agricultural technician Nar Bahadur Thapa, as well as office assistants Lakpa Tamang and Bishal Tamang, are out of contact.
With the main municipal building gone, the people’s representatives and officials are preparing to operate from Dhunche, the district headquarters of Rasuwa.

Engineer Jiban Bhatta said the immediate challenge was not only rescuing people but also reconstructing the basic machinery needed to provide relief. “Even the rural municipality’s letterhead and official stamp are gone. Collecting damage details, identifying people who need relief and carrying out administrative work have been severely affected,” he said.

The situation is even more stark in neighboring Uttargaya Rural Municipality, where the rural municipal office at Laharepauwa has disappeared along with the records stored inside. Vice-chair Chameli Gurung said the rural municipality building and the offices of wards 1 and 5 had been swept away.

“There is no telephone network and no electricity. We have no contact with anyone. We do not know who is where, and elected representatives and employees cannot contact one another. How can we work?” said Gurung. “You ask us for data. On what basis can we provide it? Please restore the telephone network and electricity first. Then we will collect the details.”

Gurung said preliminary information suggested that more than 1,000 people in Uttargaya Rural Municipality were out of contact. The loss of the municipal centre has also paralysed financial and administrative work, including allocating money for displaced people, collecting damage data and coordinating with wards. “When the municipal centre itself is gone, there is no way to carry out financial, administrative or management work,” said Gurung.

Jayaram Upreti, chief administrative officer of Uttargaya, survived after fleeing the flood, but five of his colleagues remain out of contact. He said they were caught while travelling in an ambulance to warn residents using a loudspeaker.

“While we were going around issuing the flood warning, our colleagues were caught in the flood at a place called Khalte,” said Upreti. With the office swept away, the municipality has no official documents, he said. “The employees are staying and working at the holding centers with the displaced people,” said Upreti.

The rural municipality is providing food and accommodation to around 750 people in four shelters. But the absence of roads and electricity has made it difficult to establish the scale of the damage. In some cases, parents remain missing while children have reached safety, leaving officials unable to establish complete family details.
The problem extends downstream into Nuwakot. Bidur Municipality has suffered damage in 10 wards. Municipal employee Subash Pandey said preliminary information showed 298 people out of contact.
Deputy Mayor Prabha Bogati said the municipality’s elected representatives and employees were safe and that officials were continuing to collect information on missing people.
Five motorable bridges in Bidur have been swept away, separating communities on either side of the Trishuli and making it difficult for families to reach one another.

“Until today, we focused on moving displaced people to safety and rescuing those who were stranded,” said Bogati. “The municipal disaster committee met on Friday and has started collecting details of the human and physical losses. Now we will prioritise relief and rehabilitation.”
She said the municipality had helped more than 100 students who had been unable to reach their families after a bridge was swept away to reunite with their parents.

The scale of the wider disaster has made the local governments’ predicament more serious. The Bhotekoshi flood struck Rasuwa on Wednesday morning and then moved downstream through the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers, sweeping away homes, roads, bridges and other infrastructure. By Saturday evening, police had reported 669 deaths across eight affected districts, with hundreds still missing.

Among the 15 local units declared disaster-hit by the government, Gosaikunda, Uttargaya and Kalika rural municipalities in Rasuwa, and Bidur and Belkotgadhi municipalities in Nuwakot, have suffered the heaviest human and physical losses.

The affected local governments said the damage had made it difficult to collect information on losses, arrange safe accommodation for displaced people and distribute relief. The disruption of roads, electricity and telephone services has further hampered coordination, they said.

The secretariat of Minister for Land Management, Cooperatives and Federal Affairs and General Administration Pratibha Rawal said 10 local-level employees, one rural municipality vice-chair, two ward chairpersons and two ward members were out of contact following the floods.

The Local Government Operation Act 2017 requires local governments to prepare disaster preparedness and response plans, identify and map areas at risk, take steps to protect and relocate vulnerable settlements, coordinate search, rescue and relief operations, maintain disaster-related data, and work with the federal and provincial governments, local communities, non-governmental organizations and the private sector.
With several local governments themselves severely impacted, the loss of personnel, records and basic infrastructure has made it harder for them to carry out these responsibilities.

Laxmi Pandey, chair of the National Federation of Rural Municipalities, said the federation was contacting representatives of affected municipalities and discussing how other local governments could help.

“The first priority should be to restore electricity and telephone services in the affected rural municipalities,” said Pandey. “Once communication is restored, it will be easier to contact them and provide support.”

Federalism expert Khimlal Devkota said the affected municipalities could not be expected to manage a disaster of this scale alone. “Federal and provincial governments, political parties and organizations all need to be involved,” he stressed. /dl

articles.title: They fell in love - then had to check they weren't brother and sister
articles.summary: A French couple - both conceived by sperm donors - wanted children. But with home DNA tests illegal, how could they be sure they were not related?

blocks.text: They fell in love - then had to check they weren't brother and sister
Image source, Courtesy of Audrey and Arthur Kermalvezen
Audrey and Arthur Kermalvezen met at a gathering of donor-conceived activists

For years, Arthur Kermalvezen, the child of a sperm donor, saw possible fathers everywhere he went. "I imagined it might be my teacher, the people I saw on the bus... and I was very angry because it's impossible to live like this."
When, as an adult, he fell in love with Audrey, another sperm donor baby from Paris, the question became even more pressing.
Audrey describes the moment they met at a gathering for donor conceived activists in 2010 as "love at first sight" - but was this connection a romantic or genetic attraction?
When they were born, there were only two sperm banks in Paris and many men had made multiple donations - so there was a real possibility they could be half-siblings.

Before building a life together, Arthur and Audrey needed to know whether they were related. But in France, laws governing genetic testing and donor anonymity made finding the answer extremely difficult.

blocks.caption: Image caption, It is a criminal offence to take a home DNA test in France

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
It is a criminal offence to take a home DNA test in France

In France, only a research scientist, doctor or judge can order and supervise a genetic test, and people can be fined more than €3,500 ($4,288; £3,191) for possessing a home testing kit. As a result, companies such as 23andMe, Ancestry and MyHeritage don't make their kits available in France.
Supporters of the law, in place since 1994, say it stops sensitive genetic data being given to commercial companies, and prevents family disputes being caused by unexpected results.
But Arthur points out that France is the only country in Europe that criminalises the use of such tests.

Even before her parents told her as an adult that she was donor-conceived, Audrey had qualified as a lawyer, specialising in bioethics law. Because of this, she fully understood that French law had guaranteed donor anonymity, even after a donor's death.
But Audrey had been conceived in 1979, before any such legislation existed.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Audrey and Arthur have both campaigned for the right to know one's origins

blocks.text: Audrey and Arthur have both campaigned for the right to know one's origins
While searching for other donor-conceived people born before 1994, Audrey came across Arthur. He had written a book detailing his desire to learn more about his biological origins.

Audrey says she was struck by how precisely he expressed feelings she herself had struggled to articulate. Both had loving families, yet both found themselves drawn to questions about the unknown people who had helped to create them.
When they met in person the chemistry was immediate. So was the problem.

Before they could move from platonic friendship to a romantic relationship, and even build a life together, they had to know the truth about their fathers. But no one in authority was willing to tell them.
In search of the truth

After months of searching, they found a doctor in southern France who, for €900 ($1,028; £764) in cash, conducted a genetic test which found that they were not related. But their unease remained as the doctor was breaking the law in sharing that result with them.
"We were worried he was a charlatan," Audrey says.
They considered using a home-testing kit to confirm the result, but as a lawyer, Audrey was determined to act within the law.
So, from 2010, she launched a series of legal challenges to the French system.

She wanted to know whether her donor was still alive and, if so, whether he still wished to remain anonymous. Could she access non-identifying information about how many times he had donated and whether Arthur could be among her half-siblings?
Her efforts failed.
After three years of legal challenges, the couple took a 'leap of faith' and got married.
In 2015, France's highest administrative court rejected Audrey's final appeal.

blocks.caption: Image caption, In 2013, they took a leap of faith and got married

blocks.text: Image source, Courtesy of Audrey Kermalvezen
In 2013, they took a leap of faith and got married

Shortly before the birth of their first child, a doctor agreed to investigate what information might exist about their respective donors. Under French law, a medical practitioner has access to this information about their patients, but is not allowed to share it with them.

The doctor found that their donors were born in different years - and so could not be the same man. A life-changing piece of information, but one they only gained because a doctor agreed to break the rules.
"It's completely weird," Audrey says, "because it means that the doctor can know more than me... about me."
Even with this new information, Arthur still worried they could be related, so after years of resisting it, they finally took a home DNA test.

Campaigners say the French ban has done little to stop people taking home tests, with the advocacy group DNA Pass estimating that well over a million French people have taken one. Many order them via friends in countries where they are legally obtainable - or by using forwarding services in neighbouring countries.
The test said they weren't related.
DNA shock
The DNA results soon opened more doors. After 30 years of imagining who his father might be, Arthur finally made contact with his sperm donor on Christmas Day in 2017.
But Audrey had the greatest shock. Among her DNA matches was a woman named Sophie whom she'd represented in court. The two women had been fighting for similar legal rights.
"I discovered that Sophie - a woman whose case I had pleaded in court - was my biological sister," Audrey says.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Arthur and Audrey finally built their family

blocks.text: Arthur and Audrey finally built their family
Audrey and Arthur had taken their DNA test alongside eight other donor-conceived activists campaigning for access to their origins.
Of the 10, four turned out to share the same donor: Audrey, her brother Peter, Sophie and Sophie's brother David - highlighting how real the risk of a shared donor had always been.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Today, Audrey and Arthur have three children together

blocks.text: Image source, Courtesy of Audrey and Arthur
Today, Audrey and Arthur have three children together
Many years later, a genetic match with an American led Audrey to her donor - a man called Philippe - but he had already died.
Audrey's mother wrote Philippe's family a letter, thanking them for his "gift" which she described as "immeasurable".
His family welcomed Audrey for a visit. "Everybody had tears in their eyes," recalls Audrey. Philippe's sister had never known he was a donor.

The discovery gave Audrey answers that she had sought for decades. She learned details about her biological family's medical history. She saw photographs and video footage of Philippe. "I can watch him, see how he moved and hear his voice."

Audrey's legal campaign and Arthur's book together helped drive changes to French donor-conception laws, allowing people conceived after April 2025 to access identifying information about their donors when they reach adulthood.
For now, however, France remains one of the few countries in Europe where at-home DNA testing is still prohibited.
Which means, for Audrey, the wider fight continues.
"Every person has the right to know their origins and the right to know their history," she says.
Based on an episode of The Gift on BBC Radio 4

articles.title: Norway’s new King Haakon remembers ‘dear father’ Harald in first speech as sovereign
articles.summary: New monarch Haakon VIII paid an emotional tribute to his late father, Harald V, in his first address to the nation. Vowing to follow his own path, Haakon pledged to uphold Norway’s democracy, unity…

image.caption: Norway's new King Haakon VIII during his first speech to the nation at the Royal Palace in Oslo on August 29, 2026. Image: Heiko Junge/NTB/AFP

blocks.text: King Haakon VIII of Norway paid tribute to his late father, King Harald V, calling him "such a wonderful papa" in his first address to the nation as monarch.

"Above all, you were a person who remained committed to your values and dedicated to your duties," Haakon said Saturday in a televised speech. "We greatly mourn his loss. At the same time, it gives us consolation and strength to know that there are so many who are grieving with us."

Norway's King Harald died at 89, after more than three decades on the throne, during which time he became known as a reformer and a popular monarch. In a televised speech from the palace, Haakon praised his father as a "warm and devoted family man."
Haakon became emotional while speaking about his widowed mother, Queen Sonja. He noted that his parents would have celebrated their 58th wedding anniversary on Saturday.
Norway's King Harald V dies at 89

Earlier on Saturday, Haakon met at the palace with leaders of the Church of Norway, parliament and the Supreme Court. He also received Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store, who viewed the late king’s casket after it was brought to the palace from Oslo University Hospital on Friday evening.
Flags flew at half-mast Saturday as mourners continued to gather at the palace, laying flowers alongside tributes left the previous day by more than 20,000 people.
Haakon stresses he will do things 'his own way'

Haakon said he would follow his own path, as his father did before him, while reaffirming the principles of Norway’s constitutional monarchy. He is due to swear an oath in parliament on Tuesday to uphold the country’s constitution and laws.
"We believe in our system of self-governance — and in democracy. We believe in a society built on the rule of law, where every individual has equal worth," he said.
Haakon automatically became king following his father’s death. Norway does not hold coronations, which were abolished by parliament in 1908.
But, like his father and grandfather before him, Haakon could opt for a consecration ceremony at Trondheim Cathedral, where Norwegian monarchs were crowned between 1814 and 1906.
The Norwegian prime minister told Reuters news agency that Haakon shared many of his father’s qualities, particularly his "ability to create an atmosphere of togetherness."

blocks.caption: Crown Princess Sonja and Crown Prince Harald, future King and Queen of Norway, with newly born Crown Prince Haakon in Oslo, Norway. [FILE: July 26, 1973]Image: TT/IMAGO

blocks.text: Mourning and challenges for the royal family

A national period of mourning has been declared, with no date yet set for Harald’s funeral. Churches across Norway will hold memorial services Sunday, including one in Asker, south of Oslo, which the royal family was scheduled to attend.
Harald was widely regarded as a symbol of an open and tolerant Norway and praised for leading a modern, modest monarchy.

The king had been hospitalized in Oslo since August 17 with hemolytic anemia, a condition that causes the rapid destruction of red blood cells and can lead to fatigue and shortness of breath. His health had deteriorated in recent years, forcing him to reduce his official duties.

blocks.caption: Haakon's wife, Mette-Marit, is under scrutiny for her ties to the late US sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. [FILE: 17 June, 2026]Image: PPE/IMAGO

blocks.text: The royal family has also faced a series of challenges. Haakon’s wife, Queen Mette-Marit, has come under scrutiny over her ties to the late US sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
In June, her son from a previous relationship was sentenced to four years in prison for two rapes, a sentence he is appealing.
Mette-Marit, 53, who has a serious lung disease, underwent a lung transplant in July.

articles.title: Palestinian woman and NBC News team reportedly attacked in West Bank
articles.summary:
Matt Bradley and crew assaulted while interviewing woman who said settlers had driven family out of home

A Palestinian woman and an NBC News team are reported to have been attacked and…

blocks.text: A Palestinian woman and an NBC News team are reported to have been attacked and injured by masked Israeli settlers in the Israeli-occupied West Bank on Saturday, amid worsening confrontations in the area.
Benjamin Netanyahu said he condemned the violence committed “by a handful of rioters”.
The attack occurred when four members of the news team were interviewing Aida Ahmed Abdullah and her family in the Palestinian town of Jalud, near Nablus.
Abdullah told the outlet that they had been driven out of their home by settlers, and the team was walking down a hill toward the house.
A car with Israeli license plates reversed up the hill toward them. At least four men with their faces covered leapt from the vehicle, hitting them with sticks and throwing rocks.
“They jumped out, beat us, then jumped back in the car,” said NBC News correspondent Matt Bradley. Bradley was hit twice in the arm and treated at a nearby clinic.
Abdullah, 51, was taken for medical care by the Red Crescent. Her injuries were not life-threatening. Three other members of the news team were also injured and treated.
“Suddenly a car came to us,” said producer Lawahez Jabari. “The settlers had sticks, I saw a gun, but they didn’t use the gun.”
Camera operator Khaldoon Eid said the team had not expected to be attacked in a village.
Several violent incidents in the area were reported on Saturday. Palestinian workers were pepper-sprayed in nearby Qusra by masked Israeli settlers.
Israeli security forces told the outlet they had received reports that “violent clashes had occurred, including stone-hurling toward Palestinians and additional civilians”.
They said “security forces identified dozens of rioters who had barricaded themselves inside a Palestinian home while Palestinian residents were inside”, the statement said.

“The security forces who arrived at the scene initially operated to remove the rioters from the home and separate the groups, in order to protect the residents inside. In addition, the security forces confiscated vehicles belonging to the Israeli rioters that were suspected of having been used to reach the area,” the statement said.
“IDF soldiers and Israel Border Police forces continue to operate in the areas of Qusra and Jalud to prevent further disturbances and restore order in the area,” it added.

Earlier this month, a group of settlers began blocking supplies from entering Palestinian houses on the outskirts of the village near Nablus, trapping residents inside and drawing strong criticism from the US ambassador.
Israeli forces continue to operate in the area while settlers still roam the surrounding hills.

Netanyahu, whose government has been accused of turning a blind eye to the settler attacks, condemned the “criminal acts of violence” and blamed “a handful of rioters who violate the law, cause enormous injustice to the law-abiding settler public, hinder the IDF in fulfilling its missions and harm Israel’s standing in the world”.

According to the United Nations’ office for the coordination of humanitarian affairs, Israeli forces or settlers killed 76 Palestinians in the West Bank in the year to 24 July. Three Israelis were killed over the same period.

articles.title: Turkish, Somali forces free vessel seized by pirates in Somalia
articles.summary: Turkish and Somali forces have freed the MV LUTUF after pirates hijacked the vessel off the coast of Somalia. The 10-day operation killed 14 alleged pirates and destroyed four boats used by the…

image.caption: Puntland Maritime Police Forces PMPF patrol against the pirate attacks off the coast in Puntland, Somalia [FILE: January 29, 2024]Image: Abuukar Mohamed Muhidin/Anadolu Agency/IMAGO

blocks.text: Turkey’s navy and Somali armed forces have freed a hijacked vessel in Somali waters and killed 14 alleged pirates following a battle that lasted several days, Somalia’s government said on Saturday.

"During the 10-day operation, four boats used by the pirates were destroyed and 14 pirates were killed," said a Somali Defense Ministry statement. "The sustained military pressure finally forced the remaining pirates to abandon the ship."

The MV LUTUF, a Cameroon-flagged vessel, was hijacked on August 17 off the coast of the Nugaal region of Puntland state. The joint Turkey-Somalia operation was carried out as part of a defense cooperation agreement between the two countries.

The ministry did not provide details about any casualties or the well-being of the crew aboard the vessel but said, "The forces subsequently secured the MV LATUF, which has now safely resumed its journey."
According to AFP news agency sources, at least eight members of the crew were on board, including one Turkish national.
Resurgence of piracy along Somalia’s coast
The Horn of Africa has seen a resurgence in piracy since April, according to figures from the International Maritime Organization, with at least 15 attacks off the coast of Somalia this year.
At least five cargo ships were held hostage, the most recent of which was seized on August 20 off Yemen.

blocks.caption: Maritime police patrol to ward off piracy off the coast in Puntland, Somalia [FILE: January 29, 2024]Image: Abuukar Mohamed Muhidin/Anadolu/picture alliance

blocks.text: These attacks are the highest since 2013. Piracy was rampant off the coast of Somaliain the 2000s. It peaked in 2011 before being curbed by international naval deployments and new protection measures for commercial shipping.

The resurgence of piracy in the Horn of Africa is adding to mounting challenges for international shipping in the Middle East, where vessels are already navigating around the contested Strait of Hormuz and seeking to avoid Houthi attacks in the Red Sea.
In recent years, pirate attacks have also increased along the West African coast, adding another layer of risk for commercial shipping.

articles.title: Former Ecuadorian president imprisoned for corruption
articles.summary: Lenín Moreno denies taking bribes from a Chinese firm to secure a contract to build a hydroelectric plant.

blocks.text: A former president of Ecuador has been sentenced to five years in prison after being found guilty of taking bribes.
Lenín Moreno insisted he had not taken money from a Chinese firm which secured a contract to build a hydroelectric plant in the Latin American nation.

The 73-year-old will serve his sentence under house arrest due to his age and disability, and has already indicated his intention to appeal against the verdict after a court in the capital, Quito, found him and 19 others guilty of corruption.
Moreno, who was president between 2017 and 2021, is the third former Ecuadorian leader to be sentenced for corruption.

Prosecutors alleged that that Sinohydro, which is owned by the Chinese state, paid a total of $76.1m (£56.2m) through shell companies to people involved in the deal to secure the construction of the Coca Codo Sinclair hydroelectric dam.
Among those handed prison sentences were Moreno's wife, daughter and brother, as well as former plant managers, Sinohydro representatives and a Chinese ambassador to Ecuador.
While Moreno himself was alleged to have received very little from the scheme, prosecutors said family members received tens of thousands of dollars.
Those convicted of bribery will have to repay three times what they were given, while Moreno was barred from public office.

He denied involvement in the alleged bribery scheme and instead blamed another former president, Rafael Correa, under whom he served as vice-president and who was sentenced to eight years in prison in a separate bribery case in 2020.
Moreno argued that Correa had signed off on the Coca Codo Sinclair project, and that he had launched an investigation into issues with the construction when he had assumed the presidency.

The Ecuadorian government launched legal proceedings against Sinohydro in 2021 due to cracks appearing in the dam and other technical failures. It reached a $400m settlement with the firm's owner earlier this year.
The BBC has approached Sinohydro and the Chinese embassy in Ecuador for comment.

articles.title: Norway's new king remembers 'my dear father' in first speech
articles.summary: Haakon VIII pays emotional tribute to his late father, Harald V, before outlining how he wishes to reign.

blocks.text: Haakon stressed national unity in the speech, saying the royal family believed in a "society built on law and justice, where everyone is of equal value".

He said Harald had been a good father to himself and his sister, Princess Märtha Louise, as well as a "warm and funny grandfather" to his six grandchildren and a "loving and caring husband" to his widow, Queen Sonja.
The new king appeared to choke back tears as he noted that Saturday would have been their 58th wedding anniversary.
Harald brought the family together "with a natural authority", of which he might not have been aware himself, his son recalled.
He had "always stayed true" to his "values and commitments", the new king stressed.
"He constantly reminded us in the family that each of us must do things in our own way. Find our own style. Be ourselves," Haakon said.
He also remarked on the "powerful and moving experience" of seeing thousands of Norwegians gather outside the royal palace in the capital Oslo with "flowers, tributes and candles".
"We are in mourning, yet at the same time it brings comfort and strength that so many are grieving together with us," he said.

Norwegians have been laying flowers outside the royal palace in Oslo since news broke that Harald had died on Friday. A national period of mourning has been declared, with no date yet given for his funeral.

Among them was Norway's Prime Minister, Jonas Gahr Støre, who laid flowers outside the palace and signed a book of condolences after greeting the new king, said the country was "united in grief and gratitude".

Haakon will swear an oath of allegiance in parliament on Tuesday and will later participate in a consecration service with his wife, Queen Mette-Marit - a stripped-down version of a coronation, which Norway no longer holds.
He assumes his new role at a difficult time, as the royal family has faced health challenges and scandals this year.
Mette-Marit came under scrutiny when it was revealed that she had had a three-year friendship with the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, for which she publicly apologised.

She later received a lung transplant, after suffering from pulmonary fibrosis since 2018. Doctors will not declare her stable until next year, meaning her husband must balance his new official duties with her care.
Her son from a previous relationship, Marius Borg Høiby, was convicted in June of rape and other offences and sentenced to four years in prison. He is appealing.
Høiby is not a member of the royal family, but was raised with them since he was four years old, when Haakon married his mother.
Haakon's sister, Märtha Louise, has also courted controversy for remarrying an American self-styled shaman in 2024, their business activities ultimately leading her to step back from royal duties.

Without directly referencing these controversies, Haakon said during his speech: "Our family has experienced the importance of standing together in order to remain steadfast both within ourselves and for one another even during difficult times."
He said he, along with Mette-Marit and Crown Princess Ingrid Alexandra, would "always strive to understand the life situations of different people".
He added: "No one who lives in this country knows what we will face together, but what we do know is that we will stand by one another through both good days and difficult ones."
Although Harald remained popular until his death, a poll for newspaper Aftenposten earlier this year suggested that support for the monarchy had dropped from 72% in 2024 to 54%.

However, Norwegian royal experts told the BBC that the new king, while facing questions about the turbulence surrounding his family, was respected, hard-working and, they believed, able to move forward despite the challenges.

articles.title: Australia usually hosts the world's biggest cuttlefish mating event - not this year
articles.summary: According to official figures only 1,811 cuttlefish turned up to mate this year, down 97% on last year.

blocks.text: Every winter, a sliver of the South Australian coast hosts the world's largest mating event for giant cuttlefish.

Some years, hundreds of thousands of the unique marine species endemic to Australia gather along the Cuttlefish Coast for the annual mating season, bringing their colourful, shape-shifting figures to the shallow waters and attracting thousands of keen divers.
But this year, the turnout was the lowest on record, sparking concerns of a "catastrophic decline" of the species.
Official figures released this month estimate just 1,811 cuttlefish turned up to mate this year, down from 63,000 last year - a 97% drop.
The state government says a toxic algal bloom that has ravaged the state's coastline for more than 18 months may be to blame for the sharp decline.
The low figures have also prompted calls for the species to be listed as endangered.

Adult cuttlefish typically die after breeding so each mating season is crucial for the species' future, but in recent months, just 440 eggs have been counted, instead of the millions that are usually laid.

Manny Katz, 28, was one of four divers who spent hours along the coast last month to observe the annual breeding event, having been tasked by South Australia's Department of Environment and Water (DEW).

"Because there have been so few cuttlefish, DEW thought it would be worth going out and trying to do an assessment of how many eggs there currently are around the coastline to understand what the population is going to be next year."
Over two days in July, his team did eight one-hour dives, exploring the undersides of rocky reefs to count the eggs.
"Along the eight kilometres (five miles) of coastline, there would normally be millions of eggs," he said, as each female can lay dozens of egg and tens of thousands usually turn up to breed.
"[We] pretty much looked under every single rock that we could have and we only found about 440 eggs."
While it's too early to tell what this means for the species' future, Katz said: "we will know that answer probably in the next year or two, whether or not this year has been a catastrophic decline."
His team also tracked adult cuttlefish numbers during the dive survey, and said the dozen or so they saw - when there should have been tens of thousands - appeared to be behaving differently.
"This year, they were all really skittish... hiding under rocks. Because there's so few cuttlefish hanging out at the moment, they don't have strength in numbers."
Katz said he wasn't shocked by the low numbers this winter given the devastating impact of the toxic algal bloom in South Australia since it was first detected in March last year.

The algal bloom - a rapid increase in the population of algae in water systems – is naturally occurring but is caused by ocean warming, marine heatwaves, and nutrient pollution - all exacerbated by climate change.

"Our marine habitats have been getting wiped out for the past year and a half now... this is an indicator that our marine ecosystems are in real big trouble - the canary in the coal mine, so to speak."

Last year's cuttlefish mating season was not impacted as the effects of the algal bloom had not yet reached the Cuttlefish Coast, Katz said, but since late last year, small concentrations of the toxic algae have been detected in the area.
This was particularly worrying as cuttlefish, along with other cephalopods like octopus and squid, are particularly vulnerable to the toxic algae.

Stefan Andrews, co-founder of the Great Southern Reef Foundation, is seeking to have the giant Australian cuttlefish listed as a threatened species given its "catastrophic decline" due to the algal bloom and the impact on the next generation.

"The harmful algal blooma is a leading plausible explanation and appears likely to have contributed, but the vailable evidence does not yet allow us to say definitively that it caused the entire decline," he said.
He said with so few adults and so little breeding activity observed, the number of young entering the population is likely to be very low.
"That will make the next breeding season especially challenging."
A spokesperson for South Australia's Department of Primary Industries and Regions said cuttlefish populations "naturally fluctuate" depending on environmental conditions.
Previous surveys have reported record lows of 13,500 in 2013 to highs of 247,000 in 2020.
"The cuttlefish population estimate rebounded to more than 100,000 just two years following the low numbers in 2013," the spokesperson said.

"While it appears likely the algal bloom has impacted cuttlefish numbers, researchers are working to determine whether this contributed to the reduced population or was just one of the potential impacts."

Prof Mike Steer, executive director of the South Australian Research and Development Institute which helped carry out the underwater surveys, said the unprecedented low estimate this year was "disheartening".
But he remained hopeful as "we know from the past that this population has the capacity to recover when conditions are favourable".
He said there were "positive signs" as adult cuttlefish were continuing to lay eggs and the population may recover "over coming years".

articles.title: Right-wing commentator Milo Yiannopoulos deported from US to UK
articles.summary: The self-styled provocateur had been detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

blocks.text: British right-wing political commentator Milo Yiannopoulos has been deported from the United States after being detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).
Yiannopoulos, 41, a former editor of Breitbart News and onetime political aide to rapper Kanye West, was deported on Friday, according to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS).
Yiannopoulos, "an illegal alien from the United Kingdom" had been sent "back to his home country", a DHS spokesperson said in a statement given to the BBC.
The self-styled provocateur has called himself the "most fabulous supervillain on the internet" and advocated for stricter US immigration controls. His critics call him a purveyor of hate speech.
Yiannopoulos, who grew up in Kent in the south of England, was arrested on 27 August after arriving at Louis Armstrong New Orleans International Airport.
He flew into the US in May 2019 and "chose to overstay his welcome in violation of our nation's laws", the DHS said.
He has previously cheered on ICE raids, last year calling for "total legal immunity for ICE agents when they're on duty".
He wrote on social media in 2025: "We have got to deport millions and millions of people. Without that, nothing else matters."
Yiannopoulos also advocated "on the spot deportation for anyone who can't prove they are in the US legally" on social media.
Yiannopoulos was an early supporter of Donald Trump during the 2016 election, headlining an event that year called Gays for Trump during the Republican National Convention.

The commentator has since become a critic of the US president, but still voices support for his agenda. He wrote on X in March this year that Trump had "lost his way, bought off by foreign interests".

Yiannopoulos has courted controversy with his comments on transgender people, Muslims, Black Lives Matter, feminists and gay people, even though he himself identified as gay. He now calls himself an "ex-gay".

In 2020, he assisted West in the rapper's unsuccessful bid to become president. He also worked for Marjorie Taylor Greene, a former Republican congresswoman who fell out with Trump and became a fierce critic before resigning from office.

Laura Loomer, a far-right commentator and Trump ally who has feuded with Yiannopoulos, took credit for his arrest by ICE, claiming on X on Friday night that his flight back to the UK had already departed.
"This subversive foreign agent is already out of the United States and DHS tells me he's NEVER allowed to come back to the United States ever again," she wrote.

In 2017, he was disinvited from speaking at CPAC, a US conservative conference that also hosted Trump, after footage emerged of Yiannopoulos appearing to condone paedophilia. He also later apologised and resigned from Breitbart.
He denied the allegations and said he had been speaking about his own experiences as a child.

Yiannopoulos was once regularly linked with the alt-right, a disparate group that is outspoken against political correctness and feminism, and which includes neo-Nazis and white supremacists among its ranks.
He has said he does not consider himself part of the alt-right, although he has called it "energising and exciting".

articles.title: Russian-American heads Trump's planned Caucasus trade route
articles.summary: A Russian-born businessman heads the investment fund financing the so-called "Trump Route," a planned corridor through Armenia linking Azerbaijan with Nakhchivan. Who is Konstantin Sokolov, and what…

image.caption: The proposed 'Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity' would follow the path of a former Soviet railway, near the border with IranImage: Anthony Pizzoferrato/Middle East Images/picture alliance

blocks.text: Until recently, few people in the South Caucasus had heard of Konstantin Sokolov. Now the 52-year-old Russian-American businessman is at the center of new investment fund backed by US President Donald Trump.

In mid-July, Sokolov — who emigrated from Russia to the US at age 21 and later founded the investment firm IJS Investments in Chicago — was appointed to head a new investment fund of the US State Department.

The TRIPP+ EnterpriseFund, registered in the US as the Trans-Caspian Enterprise Fund and launched with more than $200 million (about €172.5 million) in capital, is expected to invest in countries across the South Caucasus and Central Asia and help finance the large-scale TRIPP infrastructure project, also known as the "Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity."

The "Trump Route" is a transit corridor that aims to connect Azerbaijan with its autonomous exclave of Nakhchivan through Armenian territory. The ambitious infrastructure project is part of a peace deal that Armenia and Azerbaijan signed in August 2025 with US mediation. In early June 2026, Washington and Yerevan signed a framework cooperation agreement for the project.
Experts have said construction of the "Trump Route" fits Washington's strategy of creating a trade corridor between Europe and the region that bypasses existing routes through Russia and Iran.
Sokolov buys up Russian assets in Armenia
Long before he was appointed to head TRIPP+, Sokolov had already established a foothold in Armenia.

In 2024, he acquired Viva Armenia, the country's largest telecommunications provider. Despite its subsequent partial nationalization, Sokolov continued to expand his holdings. Recently, his companies also bought up the Armenian subsidiary of Russian telecom giant Rostelecom.

blocks.caption: In August 2025, Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev (left) and Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan (right) signed a joint declaration 'peace road map' after talks with TrumpImage: Azerbaijan Presidency/Anadolu/picture alliance

blocks.text: An even more significant deal, however, was carried out largely out of the public eye: the purchase of the Teghut copper-molybdenum mine. The mine, which holds an estimated 450 million metric tons of ore and has Armenia's second-largest reserves, had been taken over by Russia's state-owned VTB Bank after the company accumulated massive debts. VTB is now under Western sanctions. According to Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty's Armenian service, the deal was carried out through a third-party company.
"Sokolov wanted to avoid a direct deal with the Russian bank," said Mkrtich Karapetyan, a Radio Liberty journalist who has been investigating the flow of foreign capital into Armenia.
Sokolov: Trump supporter, MAGA backer
While Armenia's government and its supporters have welcomed the influx of Western capital into the country's infrastructure projects, the opposition has highlighted serious risks.

Mesrop Manukyan, a lawmaker from the opposition Armenia Alliance, is among Sokolov's most vocal critics in parliament. He said it's alarming that a US investor has been able to acquire major stakes in the finance, mining and telecommunications sectors in just a few years.

Manukyan's faction, which advocates close ties between Armenia and Russia, opposes the TRIPP+ project. It views the "Trump Route" as a disguised "extraterritorial corridor" and the "greatest threat" to Armenia's security.
Armenia looks to EU after decades of relying on Russia

Despite his extensive investments, Sokolov remains largely unknown to the Armenian public. There are no official photos of him, and he generally avoids interviews with the local press during business trips.

His most recent visit to the capital, Yerevan, was in early August, when he met with Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan and Foreign Minister Ararat Mirzoyan. He was accompanied by Aryeh Lightstone, senior adviser to US special envoy Steve Witkoff.

In Western media, however, Sokolov is known not only for his business ventures in the US and Switzerland but also for his political involvement. Sokolov is a major donor to the US Republican Party and a Trump supporter. According to The Associated Press, he donated about $11 million to Trump's MAGA movement over the course of a year.
'Compromise' between Moscow and Washington?
Benyamin Poghosyan of the Armenian think tank APRI sees two main reasons for Sokolov's appointment to head the fund.
